In a recent development, the ANT perpetual contract recorded $1.727 billion in trading volume over 24 hours on November 20. This has placed it second among Hyperliquid’s perpetual markets, behind Bitcoin but ahead of Ethereum.

Open interest also climbed to $259 million as traders built substantial positions rather than simply passing through short-term trades. The figures put Hyperliquid’s Anthropic market among the exchange’s most active markets, despite tracking a company outside the traditional crypto sector.

In a recent development, just a day earlier, Anthropic ranked 17th among Hyperliquid perpetual contracts by trading volume. It then climbed to second place as activity accelerated around Anthropic’s public market debut. Its $1.727 billion turnover was 1.88 times Ethereum’s trading volume during the same period. Only Bitcoin attracted more activity, recording $5.139 billion.

The shift also displays how much Hyperliquid’s trading activity now extends beyond crypto-native assets. Six of the exchange’s top ten perpetual markets by volume were linked to traditional financial assets.

In a recent development, these included Anthropic, the XYZ100 technology index, the S&P 500, Nvidia, a leveraged semiconductor ETF, and South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix. Together, those six contracts generated $4.269 billion in volume, accounting for 38.1% of the top ten’s combined turnover.

ANT’s market has also attracted significant leverage. The contract allows traders to speculate on Anthropic’s share price using crypto collateral, without purchasing or owning the underlying shares.

Unlike conventional stock markets, the perpetual contract continues trading around the clock. This gives traders a venue to react to developments outside Nasdaq’s regular trading hours. This flexibility has helped attract activity as traders position themselves around major developments affecting the artificial intelligence sector.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that parking lots should be legally required to display a sign that says "Enter at your own peril." If not so much for the property's legal nightmare, but rather for the dangerous events that typically unfold on these concrete or paved wastelands for cars. Why be afraid though when you could be like the Brits and turn a parking lot into a professional frenzy championship?

Sources indicate that the annual competition is called the Ken Wharton Autotest. Held by the Hagley & District Light Car Club, it's somewhat reminiscent of a 16-year-old's driver test, just on super steroids. According to the 2026 competition's video summary on YouTube, competitors in small cars like Mini Coopers, lightweight sports cars, and specially modified machines are "built to change direction swiftly. Outright power matters less than agility, grip and the driver's ability to put the car exactly where it needs to be." Basically, imagine Ken Block and Travis Pastrana Gymkhana performances — as a rapid time trial.

Recent findings suggest that ashley Lamont, is one of these competitors, whose absolutely near-flawless run was shared to YouTube just days ago. Lamont whipped his bright green-liveried Caterham seamlessly about the entire course in 71.3 seconds, which helped his team of Northern Ireland clinch the win for the 2026 competition.

According to recent reports, the racing competition displays a combination of motorkhana, gymkhana and American-style autocross through a competitive field set up with cones. Drivers are required to memorize the course and where their car needs to be at every turn while rapidly throwing the car from forward to reverse, back and forth (that poor transmission!) It's a timed trial as well, so the driver has to complete it as fast as possible. The fastest team can win the competition, but consistency really matters in this as well. It's mesmerizing to watch.

What that means for the audience is a wildly disorienting scene of a car being whipped around a fairly vague-looking circuit like the most eloquently-executed choreographed dance as the driver pulls 180s and J-turns without blinking. At the end of each run, you almost want them to get out of the car to take a bow after such a performance. What's unique about Lamont's run is his movement, compared to other competing drivers who sometimes pause ever so briefly before the next move, Lamont drives from flow state to flow state.

By the end, I honestly don't know who to be more impressed with, the driver, or the camera man capable of zooming in and following these cars' every move.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
HLTH 2026: Noom, Hims & Hers roll out peptide offerings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

LAS VEGAS—Direct-to-consumer health companies Noom and Hims & Hers are making a play for the peptide market as the federal government loosens restrictions on compounded treatments.

The companies are betting that peptides could be the next major thing in consumer health. For Noom, the new peptide offering extends the firm's business beyond weight loss into the broader longevity and wellness market. Hims & Hers signaled months ago that it was ready to tap into the multi-billion-dollar peptide market.

In a recent development, federal policy shifts and U.S. Food and Drug Administration enforcement discretion around compounded peptides have opened newly introduced pathways for telehealth and compounding pharmacies.

Recent findings suggest that on Tuesday, Noom launched OpenRx as a separate peptide and preventive health brand. At launch, OpenRx offers two injectable options: sermorelin, a peptide frequently prescribed for muscle support, and NAD+, a coenzyme frequently prescribed for energy. OpenRx also offers two oral dissolvable tablet options: the first formulation combines the peptides PT-141 and oxytocin with tadalafil to support sexual health. The second ODT formulation is the peptide oxytocin to support intimacy.

According to recent reports, noom indicates it plans to expand into other areas including recovery, muscle health, skin, gut health and sleep. Peptides are small pieces of protein that occur naturally in the body and help control functions such as growth, healing and appetite.

“Peptides are an crucial portion of the formulary of healthy aging,” Geoff Cook, CEO of Noom, said in a statement. “OpenRx enables our flagship Noom brand to deepen into cardiometabolic health while the newly introduced brand OpenRx supports patients with conditions too often neglected by traditional care models, like energy, muscle composition, skin health, sexual health, sleep, and recovery. Together, both brands support the same mission: to empower everyone, everywhere to live better longer – every day.”.

Noom says every OpenRx prescription is written by a licensed clinician following an evaluation of the patient’s health history, goals and clinical appropriateness. Treatments are fulfilled through Noom’s U.S.-based pharmacy network, which operates under state boards of pharmacy oversight and adheres to USP compounding standards, the firm stated.

Noom is currently reviewing BPC-157 and TB-500 as part of its ongoing process of evaluating emerging treatments for inclusion in our formulary, Jeffrey Egler, M.D., Noom's chief medical officer, noted in a statement. "Each therapy offered by OpenRx is selected because our clinical team and I believe it is appropriate for improving patient health. The process involves continuous monitoring of safety-related signals, gathering the judgment of our medical directors and the medical directors of affiliated clinical networks based on years of prescribing experience with the compounds in question, ensuring a compliant and stable supply chain, sourcing of active pharmaceutical ingredients, and setting up processes for compliance with state and federal adverse event reporting guidelines," Egler said.

Industry observers note that online health and wellness brand Hims & Hers declared earlier this month it planned to roll out a peptides business. As part of the company's latest Peptides+ specialty, introduced today, it prepares to initially sell five U.S.-compounded peptide and longevity treatments—Sermorelin, NAD+, Glutathione, Vitamin B12 and L-Carnitine, with plans to add more peptides and therapies over time.

The organization also plans to offer U.S.-made BPC-157 and TB-500 "consistent with regulatory requirements," the company stated.

Industry observers note that A survey the manufacturer conducted in October of 2,000 adults found that more than half (55%) remarked they were interested in or curious about peptide therapies, and 40% of U.S. adults say they are interested or very interested in a telehealth offering of injectable prescription treatments, including peptides and other compounded treatments. Nearly 1 in 10 U.S. adults (9%) say they right now use peptides, not including FDA-approved peptides such as Ozempic, Wegovy and insulin, the survey found.

Peptides are in the spotlight due to the massive success of FDA-approved GLP-1 weight loss medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which are peptide drugs. Wellness influencers and biohackers on social media are promoting other lab-made peptides for fast-tracked healing, anti-aging and muscle growth.

According to recent reports, health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has championed looser federal rules on trendy, unapproved peptide injections. In July, an FDA advisory committee recommended broader access to six unapproved peptides. The panel recommended adding these six substances to the Section 503A Bulks List, which would remove the restrictions on how they are produced by compounders, Fierce Pharma reported.

In a recent development, stopping short of a formal declaration allowing their use, Kennedy has cleared the way for the compounding of six popular wellness peptides, Fierce Pharma reported. Under Kennedy’s "enforcement discretion policy" issued in late October, HHS will not take enforcement action against pharmacies, physicians and federal facilities compounding six specific peptides, assuming those parties meet certain specific qualifications.

Industry observers note that but medical experts have raised safety and clinical evidence questions around unapproved or experimental compounds. The American Medical Association (AMA) publicly opposes the Trump administration’s strategy to make certain unapproved peptides more widely available for human use.

In a letter (PDF) to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the AMA pushed back what it called a "rushed" decision to permit the compounding of certain peptides because they have not been approved for safe use by the FDA.

Unproven peptides may pose serious health risks, including allergic reactions, infections, hormonal imbalances and other unexpected side effects, according to the FDA website.

According to recent reports, "We should not bypass the science and put patients at risk by making them guinea pigs for unapproved drugs," AMA President Willie Underwood III, M.D., stated in a statement. "If these substances are safe and effective, the evidence should demonstrate that through the FDA’s rigorous review process.".

Hims & Hers' peptide therapy program provides a "clinically guided, personalized plan" for consumers "backed by a licensed provider who understands these therapies," according to Anant Vinjamoori, M.D., chief medical officer of the Hims brand.

Hims & Hers wants to "set the standard" for peptide therapy and offer consistency in the quality of the products, Vinjamoori stated in an interview on the sidelines of the HLTH conference this week.

"If you think about what we have to bring to the table with our scale and resources, I would argue there's no one better equipped to do it than us," Vinjamoori noted.

Industry observers note that hims & Hers has invested in its supply chain and expanded its domestic manufacturing facilities. In 2025, the manufacturer acquired a Menlo Park peptide facility to run API validation and stability testing to support its specialized peptide offerings.

Recent findings suggest that "That's why we're investing in our supply chain and doing a lot of the hard work that, frankly, is not the fastest path to making these available. There are pharmacies that are already out there that are making these available, and there are companies out there that will simply just plug into those pharmacies and service patients. But there are inconsistencies," he noted.

Until now, getting these types of medications has often meant relying on unreliable and unregulated online sellers, or a high-cost longevity clinic, Hims & Hers executives said. Hims & Hers' peptides offering gives consumers more accessible care, "backed by real medical leadership and with consistent clinical oversight," the company said in a press release.

Hims & Hers believes its scale gives it an opportunity and responsibility to help build the evidence base around peptides, using growing patient interest not just to expand access but to better understand how the treatments can be used safely and effectively, Vinjamoori said.

It has been revealed that expanding into peptides fits with Hims & Hers' ongoing focus on personalized health, he noted. "We started with sexual health, moved on to hair loss, and then we've continued to broaden into other categories such as hormone replacement, GLP-1s, and now peptides, and many others to come. And the common theme in all of this is that we're talking about helping people accomplish a specific goal that they have. We're not talking about curing a disease or treating a disease per se," he said. "We're talking about, 'Hey, there's something you want to do in your life that you're not able to do right now. Let's help you figure out how we can put together a proposal to help you accomplish that.".

"This is a big part of the future of medicine itself," Vinjamoori added. "It's been the missing part of the equation, where we've been very focused on treating and responding to disease, but not as much, not just on prevention, but really on helping people use their health as an asset and as a tool to help them accomplish what they want in life.".

With Hims & Hers' peptide therapy offering, consumers start with a clinical visit with a licensed provider that includes a comprehensive intake of health history and goals. The tech giant remarked a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies assesses each individual and, if appropriate, tailors a personalized protocol to their needs.

According to recent reports, hims & Hers treatments are compounded in the U.S. and dispensed directly by licensed, U.S. pharmacies regulated by state boards of pharmacy and "held to rigorous quality and safety standards," the firm remarked.

The buzz around peptides ties into consumers' growing interest in taking control of their health "driven by the cultural zeitgeist moment," Vinjamoori told Fierce Healthcare.

Recent findings suggest that "There's a variety of different factors that catalyze that. I think the COVID-19 pandemic catalyzed a lot of it for a variety of reasons. I think you see accelerations in biotechnology where people now see something like GLP-1s that can help with a problem that seemed intractable before. I think people are now interested in figuring out what is the range of solutions that could help me. I also think peptides represent something that has a lot of promise, a lot of excitement," he stated.

"But there are also some cautions that we need to take as well. Something we think a lot about is how do we meet this moment of excitement and enthusiasm with some degree of rigor and guardrails," Vinjamoori mentioned.

"It starts with the product itself. How do we ensure the quality? The compounds are of the highest quality and are compounded in the most rigorous way, made available in the most rigorous way. That's why we are trying to have as much oversight as we can into the full process of making these available," he said.

He asserted that informed consent and transparency with consumers are critical. "I've spent a lot of time with the team to make sure that we understand that people have this enthusiasm, but we need to make sure that they understand what they're getting into. There is a difference between this and FDA-approved therapies," he said.

"Sometimes people should try the standard of care before they engage with some of these things, and so we want to make sure we have these conversations with people openly and honestly. But at the same time, we also want to respect their choice," he added.

Recent findings suggest that hims & Hers Peptides+ is available with its Care+ program that gives customers access to twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress, unlimited support and ongoing check-ins from a dedicated care team. Customers can also message providers trained in peptide therapy 24/7 with any questions. The Hims Men’s panel includes at-home blood collection and access to lab tests that provide insights across 22 biomarkers, including testosterone, vitamin D, and cholesterol. The Hers Women’s panel tests 22 biomarkers across hormones, vitamins, and heart health.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The home where Woodrow Wilson lived as a professor before becoming president has hit the market in Princeton, NJ for $5.85 million.
  • The Tudor Revival at 82 Library Place was built in 1896 for Wilson and he lived there with his wife, Ellen, and their three children until 1902, when he became president of Princeton University and moved on campus.
  • The home was first listed in May 2025 for $6.5 million.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The home where Woodrow Wilson lived as a professor before becoming president has hit the market in Princeton, NJ for $5.85 million.

The Tudor Revival at 82 Library Place was built in 1896 for Wilson and he lived there with his wife, Ellen, and their three children until 1902, when he became president of Princeton University and moved on campus.

The home was first listed in May 2025 for $6.5 million.

“Wilson and his wife had a lot of input in the design and finishes chosen for the home, which included double stained-glass doors from the Sears catalog,” says listing agent Barbara Blackwell of Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty.

Sources indicate that the estate is one of only two working homes in the U.S. designed and built by a president, the other being Monticello, according to the listing.

Blackwell states the house has had 19 owners since the Wilsons, including Princeton University itself, which used the home as faculty housing during the Great Depression.

The current owners spent seven years restoring the property with architect Ron Berlin and Baxter Construction. The award-winning project brought back the original beams and woodwork and re-glassed the leaded windows. It also gave the home a distinct sense of presidential charm, making it easy to imagine Wilson tucked among its interiors.

The work also restored the stucco and timber exterior, added a cedar shake roof and a generator, and updated all mechanical systems.

According to recent reports, the three-story home includes seven bedrooms and 5.5 bathrooms. Wilson once taught students in the spacious foyer, which opens to a wood-paneled library the current owners added. Stained-glass pocket doors lead to a dining room with a commissioned mural of campus landmarks.

The kitchen pairs restored original cabinetry with upcoming matching pieces. It also has a copper drainboard sink, a working dumbwaiter, and a double Wolf range. Nearby, a new glass-roofed sunroom with a wet bar overlooks the grounds.

“The sunroom is a perfect blends interior and exterior with views of the gardens and flowering trees,” Blackwell states.

In a recent development, of the four bedrooms on the second floor, one is a soundproofed primary suite with a coffee bar and a radiant-heated marble bathroom that opens onto a balcony. The skylit third floor contains three more bedrooms, a bathroom, laundry and a cedar walk-in closet.

Industry observers note that outside, the recently redesigned gardens surround two patios, a fountain and a koi pond. The 0.74-acre lot also has a circular driveway lined with boxwoods, an office in a former porte cochere and a restored, oversized two-car garage in the same Tudor style as the house.

The property is in Princeton’s Western Section and backs up to the current home of the university’s president. Nassau Street’s shops and restaurants are a short walk away.

Recent findings suggest that “This home represents a substantial piece of history with all the modern conveniences of a newly introduced home,” Blackwell indicates. The owner’s collection of Wilson books and memorabilia can be bought separately.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2050 w)

What Are The Different Classes Of Campers, RVs, And Motorhomes?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there is a wealth of choices when it comes to the types of campers, RVs, and motorhomes you can spend your free time in, so much so that you can find one of them for just about any style of camping and almost any budget.
  • It also helps to understand the different classes and types of RVs, motorhomes, and campers.
  • Next, you have towables — campers that are towed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there is a wealth of choices when it comes to the types of campers, RVs, and motorhomes you can spend your free time in, so much so that you can find one of them for just about any style of camping and almost any budget. They range from small pull-behinds that aren't much more than a step up from a tent to those mammoth rolling McMansions you see plodding along the interstate. With so many choices, how do you know which one is right for you? One place to start is our list of five things to know before you buy a used RV.

It also helps to understand the different classes and types of RVs, motorhomes, and campers. "RV" is a general term for all campers and motorhomes. "Motorhomes" refer to RVs that you can drive. There are three classes of motorhomes: Class A, Class B, and Class C. Class A motorhomes are the largest, Class B are the smallest, and Class C is in between, with some overlap in size with the other classes.

Next, you have towables — campers that are towed. This includes large travel trailers — which utilize a ball hitch linked to the towing vehicle's frame or rear bumper — bigger fifth-wheels attaching to a hitch over the truck's rear axle, and foldable campers like pop-ups and A-frames. Even though they don't have a drivetrain, slide-in truck campers aren't technically towables since they're hauled. You also have hybrid campers expanding out to the sides and rear, as well as park models, which aren't meant to do much traveling, but are designed to be towed to a spot and left there as a resort unit.

If you've ever done an interstate road trip, you've passed more than one of those behemoth RVs, usually driven by some retiree taking their time in the slow lane. The really big RVs that look like a bus are Class A motorhomes. Thor Industries says that this class can range from approximately 25 to 45 feet in length and weigh from around 12,500 to 54,000 pounds. You'll also find a maximum of four slide-outs and room to sleep up to ten people, which, frankly, is more than we could comfortably put up in our house. Some of these bad boys have a loft and a patio on the back. The Thor Aria 4000 is particularly posh, offering a spacious master bedroom, a set of bunk beds, a full stack washer and dryer, four spots for TVs (including one on the outside), and two full bathrooms — one of which has two sinks. Then you have Class A toy haulers, featuring a garage that can carry an ATV or motorcycles.

In a recent development, since Class As often have all the comforts of home, it makes sense why some luxury models can cost as much as houses in nice neighborhoods. The Newmar King Aire, for instance, is listed at over $1.7 million. Granted, that's the manufacturer's top-of-the-line luxury model. The least expensive Class A it offers, presumably for the poors, lists at over $250,000. Many Class A motorhomes are built on a commercial bus or truck chassis, and usually have a flat front end. You can find them in either gas or diesel.

Sources indicate that if you can bear to go camping without loading up everything from your house, or if you'd like to stay the night somewhere without taking up the entire back parking lot of a Cracker Barrel, then maybe Class B motorhomes are for you. They are much smaller than Class A motorhomes, usually around 17 to 24 feet in length, and weigh around 8,550 to 11,000-plus pounds, though these ranges can vary based on whom you ask. Thor states Class B motorhomes can sleep up to four people. Maybe. When it comes to the ones we've seen, sleeping four people would be pretty tight.

According to recent reports, that's not to say some models can't be fancy. The VACANZA-ion 22 comes with an impressive galley that includes a combination microwave-convection-air fryer and a nicely sized refrigerator-freezer. It also comes with AWD and a power awning with a wind sensor.

In a recent development, these RVs are also called campervans, and are typically built on a Mercedes-Benz Sprinter, Ford Transit, or Ram ProMaster chassis. Still, these are not the same as the vans that vanlifers on YouTube build out. Class B RVs are sold fresh, completely self-contained, with a bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, and running water. The vehicles DIY vanlifers usually start with are regular cargo vans that they've stuck a bed, a sink, and often a bucket into. Some of them aren't even tall enough to stand up in. In certain cases, buying a van like a Ford Transit and converting it won't save any money.

According to recent reports, so, if Class B motorhomes are smaller than Class A, then Class Cs must be smaller than Class B, right? Ha ha, no, that would be too logical. Class C motorhomes fit in between, not as big as Class A RVs, but larger than Class B RVs. If the three bears each owned RVs, Goldilocks would probably find the Class C to be just right. Class C RVs are built on cutaway truck or van chassis and usually have a sleeping compartment over the cab. The elements combine to form a distinctive silhouette. Thor indicates Class Cs run from 23 to 39 feet long and weigh about 11,000 to 32,700 pounds. As you can see, there can be some overlap in size between Class C and Class A motorhomes.

Some RVs are given the designation "Super C," but that's a marketing category, not an official class. Each manufacturer has a different definition of what a Super C is, but what they have in common is that they are essentially really large Class C motorhomes, usually on a medium- or heavy-duty commercial truck chassis. One example is the Entegra Coach Accolade. Depending on the floorplan, you could have an electric fireplace, as well as a full-size couch and a full-size dinette, not a dinette that doubles as a couch.

It's much the same with the term "B+," which is used to describe smaller Class C motorhomes that look like large Class B RVs, since they often lack the overhead compartment. They are still Class C RVs, though, because they are built on a cutaway van or chassis.

According to recent reports, most regular readers of Jalopnik know what a fifth-wheel is. We are a car website, after all. In case you don't know, a fifth wheel is a large hitch for massive trailers. You've seen a semi-truck without its trailer. That big horseshoe-looking thing on the back of it is the fifth wheel. Fifth wheels can also be installed in the beds of heavy-duty pickups, and the hitch can connect with fifth-wheel RV trailers, which tend to be pretty large.

While this references Thor's own lineup rather than a broader industry range like the previous examples, Thor indicates fifth-wheel trailers measure from 36 to 45 feet long. That means they can have more living space than even a Class A motorhome, especially if you consider the compartment that comes out over the hitch. Some of these trailers are big enough to be toy haulers, as well.

Industry observers note that but living space isn't the only advantage of a fifth wheel over a motorhome. Imagine you've backed, with great difficulty, into your camp spot, set up the chairs, grill, outside lights, mat, and other items. You rolled out the awning. Then it occurred to you that you forgot to pack plastic silverware. It's just one item, but how are you supposed to eat dinner without forks? With a fifth wheel, you don't have to pack everything back up and break down your site just to go to the store. You can just disconnect your truck, leave your trailer at the site, and go.

Industry observers note that you don't necessarily need a massive dually equipped with a fifth wheel to pull a camper around. Conventional travel trailers are made to be towed with a standard receiver hitch (frame-mounted receiver) attached to the back of an SUV or pickup, most commonly full-size. Some campers are light enough to be towed by a small car. Honda recently built a prototype of a trailer designed to be towed by EVs and small crossovers. Of course, you'll always want to check the towing capacity of your vehicle against the weight of a fully-loaded camper before trying to pull one. Travel trailers can range in size from around 15 feet all the way to over 40 feet. They can weigh as little as a couple thousand pounds or as much as nearly 14,000 pounds.

According to recent reports, the biggest ones have pretty much everything a fifth wheel has, except for the sleeping compartment that would go over a fifth wheel hitch. The smaller and mid-size travel trailers can come in a variety of shapes. You might be familiar with the small teardrop trailers. Some teardrop trailers may contain a kitchenette and a wet bath, while the smallest ones don't even have enough room to stand up in. Still, it's better than sleeping in a tent.

Prices vary wildly. Runaway Campers sells a tiny pull-behind, the CoolCamp, for just over $6,000. The 28-foot Airstream Trade Wind 27 FB is probably mid-size for a travel trailer, but is not mid-priced at almost $163,000. The 36-foot Prowler 3202DSB starts at around $42,000.

It has been revealed that if you'd like a camper that's lighter than a small conventional travel trailer, is easier to maneuver, and doesn't take up as much storage space (yet often has more room than a typical teardrop), you might look into pop-up campers. These campers stay folded down into a very compact trailer while they are stored or are being towed, and then fold out into a nice-sized living space at the campsite.

Industry observers note that traditional pop-up campers additionally extend their ends, providing two separate sleeping areas. These are soft-sided sections, meaning the experience is sort of like being in a tent, but without sleeping on the ground. Pop-up campers can come equipped with a simple toilet, shower, sink, and sometimes even air conditioning. However, basic ones lack amenities like a bathroom.

According to recent reports, another type of folding camper is the hard-sided A-frame. The roofs on these campers fold out to a point, resembling an "A", and can feel smaller than pop-ups, though they sometimes have the same amenities. Others are very simple, being just one step above a tent. Hybrid campers are a little different. Generally, they do not fold down, but they do pop out on the ends to provide more space.

In a recent development, if you've ever watched "Doctor Who," you know that the hero travels around space and time in a machine they call Tardis. On the outside, Tardis looks like a 1960s-era police call box you'd find in the U.K., but on the inside, it was a huge, multi-room ship. That's sort of the sensation you get stepping into some truck campers — they seem a lot bigger on the inside than they look on the outside, so much so that you might forget you're standing in the back of your pickup. You should take a look at the Host Cascade to see what we mean. This thing can come with, depending on your chosen floor proposal, two recliners, a sectional couch and dinette, a sizable kitchenette, a dry bath with a full shower, a bedroom, and even a simulated fireplace that is actually an electric heater. We don't mean to gatekeep, but at what point does camping stop being camping and just become staying in another house?

In a recent development, there are simpler truck campers, of course, and most are, in fact, much more modest. A dinette, a sink and stove counter, a bathroom, and a bed compartment are pretty standard for most slide-in truck campers. Some are even simpler, with a pop-up soft-side roof, a bed platform, and maybe some benches. What all of these different RV classes and types boil down to is that you've got plenty of camping choices.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • European businesses call for a robust, well-funded European Competitiveness Fund.
  • Europe is losing ground in technological leadership and struggles to scale strategic technologies, while volatile energy costs and external dependencies continue to dampen business confidence.
  • Europe’s path to enduring technological leadership relies on our ability to scale strategic technologies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European businesses call for a robust, well-funded European Competitiveness Fund.

Dear Chancellors, Prime Ministers, Presidents,.

Europe is losing ground in technological leadership and struggles to scale strategic technologies, while volatile energy costs and external dependencies continue to dampen business confidence.

Europe’s path to enduring technological leadership relies on our ability to scale strategic technologies. By stabilising energy costs, providing a path to clean industrial renewal and cultivating European resilience, we are laying the groundwork for robust business and investors’ confidence. Public investment has a crucial role to play to address these vital challenges. We require a smarter, more strategic investment policy for Europe.

We, more than 75 undersigned businesses, call on European leaders to agree to a Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) commensurate with Europe’s challenges, to protect its investment capacity and place long-term productivity growth, resilience and decarbonisation at its core. We believe the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) represents a step-change in the EU’s investment policy and must be strengthened in the remaining negotiations.

Sources indicate that the ECF with its toolbox projects the ambition to provide tailored support to the investment and scale-up challenge Europe faces. This is a positive evolution of the EU funding landscape. With a bigger role for the EU’s derisking instrument InvestEU, the ECF can become Europe’s modern investment vehicle with an increased use of guarantees, loans and equity to unlock strategic investments.

At the same time, non-repayable support needs to be dedicated to scaling up sectors that deliver high strategic value but cannot yet secure commercial capital in Europe. Ramp-up support for Europe’s cleantech manufacturing, including support for OpEx, is needed to make Europe’s bid to regain technological leadership credible.

The advisory services for SMEs and the single access portal promises a simpler access to funding for firms across Europe. If successful, the ECF can pool additional national funds through merit-based procedures open to eligible projects across the single market to bring further alignment and synergies into European industrial development.

Europe’s energy import dependency has become a strategic vulnerability for European businesses. To increase our economic resilience, the EU must prioritise investments into energy sovereignty. Incentives need to pivot capital allocation away from fossil fuel infrastructure, and towards clean energy and electrification. From 2028, the next MFF should not support new fossil-fuel infrastructure that prolongs dependency on fossil fuels, while providing narrowly defined safeguards for security of supply. We need steering mechanisms to reduce fossil fuel dependencies. EU funding can help to tackle high upfront costs and derisk the switch to cleaner and more reliable energy. Otherwise, long investment cycles create severe fossil fuel lock-in effects that threaten our operational autonomy with increasingly volatile fossil energy prices.

Europe’s investment gap cannot be solved by a smarter, more strategic funding approach alone. The confidence into European competitiveness needs to translate into a sizable budget for the clean transition to have lasting impact. The Commission proposes an average annual budget of €3.3 billion for a clean transition and industrial decarbonisation window of the ECF. This number is dwarfed by recurring estimates of the annual climate investment deficit of €344 billion. At the same time, according to the OECD, industrial subsidies have reached the highest levels since the financial crisis 2008.

In a recent development, we urge European leaders to respond to the evolving investment environment and adopt the European Parliament’s proposal to increase the size of the ECF by €26.6 billion and to allocate a substantial share of the additional funding for industrial decarbonisation and clean transition. The more efficient use of financial instruments and a strategic prioritisation can improve the impact of EU funding but cannot substitute the investment needs Europe is facing to boost competitiveness and security.

The next long-term budget and the European Competitiveness Fund must become the investment trigger for European businesses to regain competitiveness at the global scale, based on clear incentives and regulatory certainty. We businesses urge leaders to demonstrate a long-term vision and make the ECF the cornerstone of a fresh EU green industrial strategy.

HLTH 2026: Viz.ai executive shares lessons from effort to expand AI adoption at rural hospitals" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

It’s been almost seven months since artificial intelligence disease detection and care coordination platform Viz.ai entered into a partnership with the National Rural Health Association (NRHA).

Recent findings suggest that the partnership aims to help rural healthcare leaders better understand and implement AI tools across systems. That's been a personal and professional passion of Viz.ai Chief Clinical Officer Andrew Ibrahim, M.D., who discussed with Fierce Healthcare at HLTH his key takeaways from the collaboration thus far and forward-looking goals as it approaches its one-year mark.

Sources indicate that ibrahim mentioned that the two organizations have done three educational events for rural health systems since the partnership kicked off in April. These series aim to show rural health administrators the specifics of AI—and whether they should adopt it, he said.

He noted there’s “sometimes a very substantial mismatch” when smaller rural health systems onboard multiple vendors.

“We've learned [that] many rural hospitals don't have the IT expertise and infrastructure to adopt some of these tools, and so it's actually been a force function to strengthen their hub spoke relationships,” Ibrahim stated.

Strengthening these relationships, according to Ibrahim, has been key.

“It's actually been beautiful to see the hub-spoke relationship strengthened with the AI tool as the conduit,” Ibrahim said. “And it gives them a reason to interact more, and a way for the rural hospitals to strengthen their capabilities.”.

He continued, “there's an authenticity about the moment where it's like ‘Yeah, we do need to help each other out.’ We're all kind of figuring it out as we go.”.

In addition to the educational series, Ibrahim remarked frameworks are in development to aid rural health systems in navigating, implementing and deploying AI—which will be built into a toolkit.

One of Ibrahim’s personal goals for the one-year mark of the partnership is to ensure any rural health administrator can understand what an AI tool is when pitched.

According to recent reports, “I think that would be a huge milestone,” he stated. “Getting to 100% of hospitals at year one would be ideal—probably unrealistic, but that's probably the ultimate goal.”.

And when it comes to metrics for measuring the collaboration, Ibrahim noted he's looking for numbers that show participants are “keeping more care local” and retaining their workforces.

“It would be great to be able to connect the dots [and understand whether] adoption of an AI tool give[s] rural clinicians confidence, enthusiasm, willingness to stay in their community as opposed to dropping the services and moving back,” he said.

Another initiative from Viz that has “disproportionate benefit in rural communities,” according to Ibrahim, is its new partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to integrate the Viz.ai One platform into UpToDate Expert AI.

“I'm pretty excited about being able to bring their level of clinical decision support into our rural hospitals,” he said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Department of Labor moves to end expedited green cards for nurses, physical therapists" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Industry observers note that the U.S. Department of Labor proposed latest policy this week that would end fast-track green cards for healthcare professionals like nurses and physical therapists—the latest in a string of policies from the Trump administration raising the bar for foreign-born workers and students across healthcare and other industries.

Right now, nurses, physical therapists and other workers “with exceptional ability in the sciences or arts” are granted an exemption from an administrative test in the permanent labor certification program (PERM), a months-long administrative process in which an employer must prove there are no able, willing, qualified and available U.S. workers for a permanent job ahead of sponsoring a foreign worker.

The exemption, referred to Schedule A, is given to occupations where the DOL recognizes a nationwide shortage of U.S. workers. Nurses and physical therapists have been listed under Schedule A for more than 30 years.

The Department of Labor, in its newly proposed rule, stated it wants to eliminate Schedule A as it cannot “demonstrate that the occupations right now listed in Schedule A are still shortage occupations.”.

According to recent reports, it cited in the proposed rule a late 2023 request for information published under the Biden administration seeking input on potentially expanding Schedule A. Despite more than 2,000 responses, DOL now indicates it didn’t receive the information it would need to establish a methodology for regularly reviewing and updating Schedule A occupations, and questioned whether it has the statutory authority to make such occupational exemptions in the first place.

It has been revealed that “The elimination of Schedule A would enable the Department to better ensure that U.S. workers have an opportunity to apply for available job opportunities, and adhere to the statutory requirements to protect U.S. workers assigned to it, as intended by Congress under the [Immigration and Nationality Act].”.

The proposed rule, which is open to public comment for 60 days, also includes requirements for employers to advertise their open jobs more broadly and for a longer period of time to demonstrate a good-faith effort to recruit American workers before turning to a green card sponsorship. These and other proposed changes would be the first “comprehensive” reforms to the PERM program in almost two decades, the Department of Labor mentioned.

If finalized as-is, employers who want to sponsor professional nurses, physical therapists and other affected roles “would be required to go through the lengthier and costlier PERM labor market testing process, adding time, cost and administrative work to a pathway that hospitals, nursing homes and rehabilitation providers have historically relied on to fill persistent shortages,” Caroline Tang, an Austin shareholder at labor and employment law firm Ogletree Deakins, told Fierce Healthcare.

Industry associations as well as other sections of the government have widely projected shortages in the healthcare workforce, including nurses, for the coming years. The Heart Resources and Services Association’s National Center for Health Workforce Analysis, for instance, projects (PDF) national shortages of registered nurses through at least 2038, with a projected 8% shortage in 2028 that is more severe in non-metro areas.

The proposed policy change is among several brought by the Trump administration in line with an order from the White House to prioritize domestic hiring—though many have been stymied in the courts.

It has been revealed that among the most prominent is a $100,000 supplemental fee the Department of Homeland Security attached to H-1B petitions that was vacated by two separate judged, and in August was succeeded by the somewhat altered proposal of an additional H-1B petition fee of $103,265. Another policy from the same department tightening how long nonimmigrant students may remain in the country (referred to as “duration of status”) was temporary blocked hours before implementation in September and fully vacated on Monday (PDF), though the former decision is already being appealed.

The Department of Labor has also proposed increasing the prevailing wage floors for several green cards that legal experts expect will be challenged by employers that would shoulder the resulting financial burden.

#167994. Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (989 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A smile might brighten your mood, but upcoming research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect.
  • For years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier.
  • "I used to work in customer service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A smile might brighten your mood, but upcoming research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect. When smiling becomes an obligation, especially one tied to financial pressure, it may actually leave people feeling less happy and more irritated.

For years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier. Yet those findings never quite matched his own experiences.

"I used to work in customer service. I actually got written up for my inability to keep smiling at work at an unnamed theme park in Florida," laughed Coles, a professor of psychology at the University of Florida. "So I'm looking at all this evidence I had accrued so far that smiling boosts happiness and realizing it flies in the face of my own experiences in the world.".

That contradiction inspired Coles and his colleagues to investigate what happens when people must keep smiling, rather than simply trying it once. Their findings suggest an key distinction: A brief, intentional smile can provide a small emotional lift, but repeatedly putting on a smile under pressure can undermine happiness.

Testing How Forced Smiling Affects Happiness.

To explore this difference, Coles worked with researchers Annabel Dang and Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi to design an experiment that more closely resembled the demands of customer service jobs. Their findings were published on October 1 in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

It has been revealed that "We tried to combine the classic way of studying it in a lab with some extra ingredients that we might see in the real world. We told participants that we would pay them less if they weren't successfully smiling," Coles noted. "We also controlled the number of times they have to do it, because in customer service, every interaction is another faked smile.".

According to recent reports, the online experiment initially enrolled 1,201 people, with data from 1,174 included in the final analysis. Participants were shown images designed to produce different emotional reactions. Some depicted appealing subjects, such as kittens and flowers, while others showed disturbing situations, including theft and mistreatment of animals.

According to recent reports, during the experiment, participants either deliberately formed a smile or allowed their facial expressions to develop naturally. Depending on their assigned group, they completed the exercise once or repeated it 10 times.

To introduce an element of pressure, researchers warned half the participants that failing to follow the smiling instructions could cost them $2 from their $6 payment. However, nobody actually lost any money, and every participant received the full amount.

When Fake Smiles Start to Backfire.

After completing each task, participants reported how happy they felt. The results revealed that the emotional effects of smiling depended on how often people had to do it and whether they felt pressured.

Industry observers note that when participants viewed unpleasant images, producing a single smile gave their mood a modest boost. This benefit appeared even among those who had been warned about a possible financial penalty. However, the positive effect weakened when smiling was repeated, and it disappeared when repeated smiles were combined with the threat of losing money.

According to recent reports, the pattern was even more revealing when people looked at pleasant pictures. Smiling just once offered little additional happiness compared with allowing their faces to respond naturally. But when participants had to smile repeatedly or felt pressure to do so, their happiness ratings actually fell below those of people who responded naturally.

Sources indicate that further analysis revealed another unexpected consequence. In the pleasant picture conditions, forced smiling was also associated with increased irritation and anger.

Sources indicate that "If you only force a smile once without any financial penalties, you can see the improvement in happiness. So what psychologists were seeing in their lab is right," he noted. "But when you make it a little bit more like the real world, where you have to keep repeating it, and if you don't do it well, you get financial penalties, you see it completely reverse.".

The Hidden Emotional Cost of Smiling at Work.

These findings may help explain why expectations to appear cheerful throughout the workday can become frustrating rather than uplifting.

The issue has already sparked controversy in the workplace. In recent years, Target faced widespread criticism over a policy requiring employees to smile when customers came within a specified distance. Although the policy was intended to encourage friendly interactions, Coles argues that such requirements can interfere with people's ability to express their emotions naturally.

The problem may extend beyond employees. Customers can also feel obligated to respond positively to friendliness that is being imposed rather than offered spontaneously. According to Coles, these expectations limit the emotional freedom of both sides of the interaction.

Could Trying Less to Be Happy Make Us Happier?

After spending years investigating how people can improve their emotional well-being, Coles has begun considering a broader question. Rather than constantly searching for ways to increase happiness, might people be better off placing greater value on simply being content?

His research suggests that efforts to manufacture positive emotions do not always produce the intended results. Sometimes, trying too hard to appear happy can make the experience less pleasant.

"As a society, we have placed such an immense amount of emphasis on trying to make ourselves feel happier than we currently are," he mentioned, "much less emphasis on just being content with what we have.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) is an interesting piece of legislation. It is getting a ton of support from the solar sector, but it is heavily opposed by environmental organizations.

Following the passage of BAAJA in the US Senate the other day, Tim Pawlenty, CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), stated the following: “America is now one step closer to lower energy costs, more clean energy and a more reliable electric grid. Senators Lee, Capito, Heinrich, and Whitehouse deserve tremendous credit for advancing this bipartisan bill.”.

The organization adds some more detail and why it thinks this is such a good piece of legislation: “SEIA analysis shows that BAAJA could unlock 167 gigawatts of additional solar capacity between 2028 and 2035, bringing solar to over 18% of U.S. electricity generation by 2035. The analysis finds that the bill’s reforms could reduce cumulative power sector CO2 emissions by approximately 20% and avoid $54 billion in public health damages.”.

It has been revealed that that sounds very appealing, doesn’t it? Why wouldn’t we want that?

It has been revealed that well, the Sierra Club argues the bill goes in quite the opposite direction. The storied organization states the following: “While a rogue president is waging a war on clean energy, the Senate rushed a deeply flawed bill that furthers the buildout of fossil fuels, strips away power from communities and Tribes, threatens our clean water and public lands, and endangers wildlife. The House of Representatives has an equal voice in the legislative process. They must reject the Senate’s fast-tracked bill and demand debate and consideration to deliver for the people, not corporate polluters and Donald Trump. The American people made a clear call merely weeks ago: our elected leaders must address soaring costs and a corrupt system that prioritizes corporate polluter profits over our health, our wallets, and our future.”.

It seems the issue is that BAAJA would make it much easier to put up power plants, skipping all kinds of environmental protections. That is why Republicans support it in the first place — they are always keen to plow through environmental protections. The reason SEIA supports it is clear enough — the organization is just thinking about solar power plants and looking at the potential for more growth in the industry, especially considering the fact that solar is now typically the cheapest option for newly introduced power capacity and has been dominating new installations.

So, the question is: would BAAJA really disproportionately support solar power, or would it lead to a lot more fossil fuel power plants and an edge to the old, dirty power technologies? Can the legislation be both good and bad, or is someone getting this wrong?

UnitedHealthcare is teaming up with CPSEN for a latest program that will lean on community pharmacists to reach Medicaid patients.

The insurance giant remarked Wednesday that its through the UHC Pharmacy Care Hub model, pharmacists will work alongside the payer's care managers and providers to help close gaps in care and support management for chronic conditions and other needs.

Participating pharmacies will offer a range of services, including telehealth, medication management, point-of-care testing and personalized supports. The program is built on a hub-and-spoke model, where pharmacists can then help lead the patient to the right site of care or through any follow-up if needed.

These interactions can also help track patterns in emergency care use, and help patients find a more appropriate setting if their needs aren't emergent.

Recent findings suggest that the program is at the moment available to UnitedHealthcare Medicaid members in seven states: Florida, Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia. UHC expects to add additional states throughout the year.

Part of the goal, the company said, is to tap into the trust that local pharmacists have in the communities they serve.

Recent findings suggest that “Community pharmacies are trusted, local access points for care,” remarked Arethusa Kirk, M.D., chief medical officer for UnitedHealthcare Community & State, in the announcement. “This new model expands the services independent pharmacists can help deliver, making it easier for people—especially those facing barriers to care—to get timely support closer to home.”.

Sources indicate that UHC said that most (89%) of Americans live within five miles of a pharmacy, making these locations an easier option to access for many. This is especially true for individuals who may struggle to find an appointment with a doctor or find transportation to a visit.

For example, a participating pharmacist in North Carolina, Madeline Clark, said in the announcement that a patient came into the pharmacy for a urine test, as she had a potential urinary tract infection. The pharmacy conducted the test and sent the results virtually to a provider through UnitedHealthcare's Doctor Chat tool.

A prescription was then filled for the patient in the same visit, and she was out the door within about 30 minutes.

Clark remarked the patient was thankful not just for the ease of that trip to the pharmacy but for avoiding a visit to the ER as well.

"Not only was this a lower cost of care in the healthcare system space, but it also was just incredibly helpful for the patient," she noted.

Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (983 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but newly introduced research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference.
  • Recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected.
  • Medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but newly introduced research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference. A clinical trial led by researchers at La Trobe University found that supervised exercise and education can improve knee health, reduce pain, and enhance quality of life in young adults recovering from anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. The findings also offer hope for addressing their elevated risk of developing knee osteoarthritis at an unusually young age.

Recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected. About half of patients are still dissatisfied with their knee health two years after the procedure. Even more concerning, roughly half develop signs of early-onset knee osteoarthritis within a decade, often before reaching age 40.

Medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations. One obstacle is the widespread concern, shared by some patients and healthcare professionals, that exercise could damage already vulnerable knee cartilage.

A New Approach to Recovery After ACL Surgery.

To investigate whether additional rehabilitation could help, researchers at La Trobe University's Sport and Exercise Medicine Research Centre conducted the SUPER-Knee clinical trial. It was the first study to evaluate the benefits of combining exercise therapy and education more than nine months after ACL reconstruction, a time when patients are generally expected to have recovered even though many continue to experience problems.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers enrolled 184 adults between the ages of 18 and 40 who were still struggling with knee symptoms one to three years after their operations. Participants were assigned to either a progressive exercise therapy program or a comparison group that received a single educational session.

The findings, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, revealed that participants who completed the four-month program under the guidance of a physical therapist experienced improvements in knee health and muscle strength, along with less pain and better quality of life.

Importantly, these benefits came without evidence that the exercises were damaging knee cartilage or worsening early osteoarthritis. The results challenge the belief that physical activity necessarily makes injured knees worse.

Exercise Offers Hope Against Early Knee Osteoarthritis.

Associate Professor Adam Culvenor, who led the research, said the findings provide much-needed evidence about how to help younger patients who remain at risk of knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery.

In a recent development, "Presently we don't have any high-quality evidence for what treatments should be offered to young people at risk of early-onset knee osteoarthritis. Our SUPER-Knee study changes this, and addresses a globally recognized research priority," Associate Professor Culvenor said.

"Our study highlighted physiotherapist-supervised exercise therapy and education is safe and should be recommended to improve the knee health of young people at high risk of early-onset osteoarthritis following ACL reconstruction.

"The evidence generated by the SUPER-Knee trial can be used to patch international clinical practice guidelines for rehabilitation following ACL reconstruction and could be a lifeline for young people struggling after serious knee injuries.

"The intervention is ready to be used by local health professionals with minimal specialized equipment or staff training.".

The findings could influence how clinicians approach rehabilitation long after ACL surgery, particularly for patients whose symptoms continue beyond the usual recovery period. Although the trial did not establish whether the program prevents osteoarthritis over the long term, it demonstrated that supervised exercise can improve knee health without accelerating the cartilage damage or early osteoarthritis researchers were monitoring.

Years of Knee Pain After a Serious Sports Injury.

Industry observers note that for Ruby Cumming, the challenges of recovering from ACL surgery were deeply personal. In 2019, when she was 24, she tore her ACL while playing Australian rules football. Hoping to return to the sport as quickly as possible, she underwent reconstructive surgery within six weeks.

It has been revealed that but the operation did not lead to the recovery she had imagined. Her rehabilitation continued for years, and she ultimately decided not to return to football.

"I thought if I had the surgery and did the rehab I'd be able to get back to normal. After surgery impacted my entire life - not just footy - I changed my outlook and decided I wanted to avoid re-injuring my knee ever again so haven't played contact sport since," Ruby noted.

"Experiencing regular pain, not being able to walk, getting public transport to work and living independently all became really challenging for me.".

Sources indicate that cumming remained committed to her rehabilitation, regularly attending physical therapy appointments and performing prescribed exercises. She initially exercised daily before moving to a weekly routine. Despite those efforts, she continued to experience varying degrees of knee pain every day for three to four years.

Her experience changed after she enrolled in the SUPER-Knee trial and began participating in weekly rehabilitation sessions supervised by a physical therapist.

"When I joined the SUPER-Knee program and did weekly physio-supervised rehab, this improved my pain significantly," Ruby said.

The research suggests that people who continue to struggle after ACL reconstruction may benefit from additional structured rehabilitation, even years after their original injury. Because the program requires little specialized equipment or additional staff training, researchers say healthcare professionals could readily incorporate it into existing treatment services.

The SUPER-Knee clinical trial received funding through a Project Grant from Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC).

The LiTime Lares K1 Expandable Plug & Play Kitchen Backup — CleanTechnica Tested

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1247 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I spent 35 years in the Tampa suburbs, so I pay attention to backup power when a storm  is coming.
  • Recent findings suggest that liTime launched the Lares K1 in the US on October 20, 2026.
  • It has been revealed that the inverter puts out 2,000 watts continuously and 4,000 watts of surge power for one second, as a pure sine wave at 120 volts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I spent 35 years in the Tampa suburbs, so I pay attention to backup power when a storm  is coming. Last year I tested the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 portable power station for CleanTechnica. That unit is meant to be carried around. The LiTime Lares K1 is different: a plug-in kitchen backup battery you leave in place and hook up to a refrigerator and also use to power your small kitchen appliances. First I’ll go through the specs and how it compares with a portable station like the Elite 100 V2, then I’ll give my test results.

Recent findings suggest that liTime launched the Lares K1 in the US on October 20, 2026. It is a split system: a slim inverter charger paired with a separate 2,304 watt-hour LiFePO4 battery (51.2 volts, 45 amp-hours). You can add up to four batteries, which brings the total to 9,216 watt-hours. The battery is rated for 4,000 cycles, and LiTime backs it with a 5-year warranty.

It has been revealed that the inverter puts out 2,000 watts continuously and 4,000 watts of surge power for one second, as a pure sine wave at 120 volts. Adding batteries does not raise that output. You just get more runtime. There are two AC outlets, one on each side of the inverter. I did not see any USB ports listed.

You can charge it at up to 1,500 watts from a wall outlet and up to 800 watts from solar (12 to 60 volts). Combined input is capped at 1,500 watts. LiTime does not put a charge time on the main product page. If you divide 2,304 watt-hours by the 1,500-watt wall input, you get about 90 minutes from empty to full. That is a rough estimate. Charging usually slows down as you get close to 100%, the same way an EV does, and their FAQ later puts the theoretical time at about 1.7 hours if you figure 90% charging efficiency.

In a recent development, the inverter charger weighs about 10.1 pounds. LiTime does not list the battery weight, but I weighted it after I took it out of the packaging and it was about 52 pounds. With the floor stand, the two modules stood up together are 20.47 inches wide, 30.71 inches tall, and 3.94 inches deep. It runs at about 40 decibels (which is very quiet) and switches over to battery in 10 milliseconds or less. It has a touchscreen, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.0, and the LiTime app, plus a time-of-use mode so you can charge off-peak.

It has been revealed that the price on LiTime’s site is $1,099.99, shown as $100 off. US preorders opened October 20, 2026, and when I checked, estimated delivery was November 24 to 27.

Recent findings suggest that liTime calls this “space-based” home backup. Instead of trying to power the whole house, you protect one room, in this case the kitchen. You plug the system into a wall outlet and plug the fridge into the K1. No electrician and no panel work. LiTime estimates about 24 hours of backup on a large side-by-side refrigerator (while I got a bit more than that in my testing) that uses about 2 kilowatt-hours a day, or about 99 hours with four batteries if the fridge is the only load. Depending on the load, it can also run a microwave, an air fryer, a toaster, or a coffee maker for a basic meal. Just don’t try to run them all at once. You can run two smaller loads at once, but a large load like a microwave or air fryer needs to be run by itself (you can keep your refrigerator plugged in too). LiTime states to allow for compressor startup if you also want to run one of those at the same time.

According to recent reports, you can wall-mount it, stand it on the floor, or lean it against a wall, with the two modules together or apart. It comes with mounting hardware and two connection cables, 0.25 meters and 1.5 meters (about 10 inches and 5 feet). The battery housing is steel, and LiTime notes the metal finish is meant to suit a kitchen. The inverter is rated IP20, so it stays indoors. LiTime says separating the inverter from the battery cuts down on heat transfer, which they claim helps the battery last longer. I have not measured that.

According to recent reports, for a plug & play system, this is a new product category. There have been portable generators available for years that could be used for camping or appliance backup, but having a product tailored to a specific room is a new concept. The comparison they offer is this one-room approach versus a whole-house battery system, the kind that usually needs panel work and that will cost you about 10 times as much.

According to recent reports, you can use this for camping or travel, but it isn’t built for it. With split modules, wall-mount hardware, only two AC outlets, and no USB ports, this is built for a permanent kitchen install, not something you toss in the car for a weekend trip.

Recent findings suggest that I used my old Kill-A-Watt meter to have an independent measure of the draw on the battery from the refrigerator. During the test, I opened the refrigerator less than I normally would, but still opened it about 10 times.

Next I wanted to test it with my small kitchen appliances. First, one at a time; then, several at once. It is rated at 2000 watts continuous, but it should be able to surge up to 4000 watts for 1 second.

Notice that it pulls 2510 watts from the battery, but the load is only 2290 watts. Where did the other 220 watts go? That must be used by the inverter to convert DC to AC.

After 35 years of Tampa storm seasons, I’ve learned that the fridge is usually the first thing you worry about when the power goes out. The LiTime Lares K1 is built for exactly that. In my testing it kept our large side-by-side GE refrigerator running for almost 26 hours on one battery, a bit longer than LiTime’s own estimate of 24 hours. It then shut off cleanly to protect the appliance. Recharging from the wall took about 3 hours, with 80% back in about 2 hours.

It also handled my small kitchen appliances well. The air fryer, coffee maker, and refrigerator ran together at about 2,200 watts, a little over the rated 2,000. When I added the toaster to push it past its limits, it briefly put out about 3,140 watts and then dropped back to about 2,130 watts without shutting down. The app also demonstrated about 220 watts lost in converting battery power to AC, which is worth keeping in mind when you estimate runtime.

Recent findings suggest that it does have limits. There are only two outlets, no USB ports, and the battery weighs about 52 pounds, so this is a permanent kitchen install, not a camping generator. Adding batteries gives you more runtime, but not more output.

At $1,099.99, with no electrician or panel work needed and a 5-year battery warranty, the Lares K1 is an affordable way to protect your food and still cook a basic meal during an outage. It costs about a tenth of what a whole-house battery would. If kitchen backup is what you care about most, it’s well worth a look.

Aetna unveils new program aimed at offering end-to-end support for moms and babies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Aetna is rolling out a new program that aims to provide key end-to-end care for pregnant women, new mothers and infants.

According to recent reports, the offering, called Aetna For You and Baby, will be available to all expectant mothers enrolled in an Aetna blueprint. Through the program, moms will be connected to a prenatal visit in their first trimester and a postpartum visit within 12 weeks of the baby's birth.

Women in the program will also be screened for depression both during and after pregnancy to identify any risks.

In addition to supporting the mother both during pregnancy and postpartum, the program aims to give babies a healthy start by providing at least six well visits through their first 15 months, which offer critical tests and screenings, checkups and vaccinations.

The news of the launch was provided first to Fierce Healthcare.

Katerina Guerraz, Aetna's chief operating officer, told Fierce that maternal care often focuses mostly, if not completely, on labor and delivery, though prenatal and postpartum visits play a critical role in driving positive health outcomes.

In its announcement, Aetna notes that data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that about 90% of pregnancy-related deaths could have been prevented, with a lack of access to prenatal care and more complete support making for a key barrier.

"This is a national access matter, a quality issue, and it's an affordability problem," she remarked.

In addition, it's not uncommon for programs that aim to drive better maternal outcomes to lack services for the babies, who in the first year of life undergo a wide array of critical developmental milestones, Guerraz said.

According to recent reports, aetna, as the third-largest insurer in the U.S., sees about 200,000 deliveries a year among its members. That means the success of this program could have a significant impact in a short amount of time, supporting at least 1 million babies over the next five years, she noted.

Aetna for You and Baby also builds on a broader push within the tech giant to build a more personalized and simple experience for members. For instance, the company established a program that embeds Aetna nurses in the hospital to support discharge planning and transitions for members, and Guerraz mentioned that holds potential in the maternal care space.

For example, if a baby needs to stay in the neonatal intensive care unit after birth, having an Aetna nurse in the NICU providing additional support to the clinical team and the member would pay dividends, she said.

Aetna is also plugged into Health 100, a sister subsidiary of its parent company, CVS Health, that offers an AI-powered tool to help patients identify healthcare costs and navigate their benefits, even if they're not members of Aetna or Caremark or CVS Pharmacy customers.

Guerraz said the program is designed to offer something that patients can carry with them if their coverage changes.

She added that the team intends to continue iterating on the program and identifying other barriers to care for moms and their babies.

"This is something that we know is going to have a massive impact," she remarked.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The coming week brings a number of key indicators and new research from the Realtor.com Economics team, despite the holiday schedule for Thanksgiving Day.

On Monday, new research from senior economist Hannah Jones shows that many Americans won't be traveling far to visit their parents for the holiday. That’s because a third of American adults under 35 years old still live in their parents’ home.

On Wednesday, senior economist Jiayi Xu has our third-quarter International Demand report, showing where home shoppers from different countries are looking at U.S. homes.

Also on Wednesday, coming out early due to the Thanksgiving holiday, senior economist Jake Krimmel will analyze our weekly housing data for clues on the latest housing market trends in real time.

For economic indicators being released next week, we’ll see the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Index on Tuesday, along with new-home sales and the Freddie Mac mortgage rate on Wednesday.

Industry observers note that the Case-Shiller Index is expected to show national home price growth holding near 2% through September, after the national index rose 2.1% year over year through August. Annual gains have climbed since the spring, but slower median sales price growth and softer contract activity this summer suggest the pickup may be running out of steam.

Recent findings suggest that new-home sales are likely to show another weak month in October, after falling 5.3% year over year in September. The existing-home segment saw softer pending home sales and home purchase closings last month as buyers are faced with affordability challenges due to high mortgage rates.

Despite more builders offering mortgage rate buydowns, the new-home segment is expected to be slowed down as well, as buyers’ budgets are stretched thin.

One thing I’ll be watching closely is the median fresh-home sales price, which has been lower than the median existing-home sales price for much of 2026, an intriguing result that mostly stems from where the new homes being sold are located.

The Freddie Mac average mortgage rate, which will come out on Wednesday instead of its usual Thursday, is likely to remain in the low-7% range, as the 10-Year Treasury yield remains elevated above 5% in advance of the expected rate hike by the Federal Reserve.

For full reports, the Market Clock, and raw housing data, visit realtor.com/research.

Joel is a senior economist at Realtor.com. He earned a bachelor’s degree in economics and mathematics from Baylor University and a master’s in economics from the University of Texas. His career has focused on the intersection of technology and real estate, and Joel has appeared live on CNN, Yahoo Finance, and Fox 7 Austin.

A surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math
