Recent findings suggest that fierce Healthcare is tracking workforce changes across healthcare in 2026. Stick with this tracker for the latest updates, and reach out to the team with any layoff news. Also, take a look back at our trackers for 2025 and 2024.

RWJBarnabas Health disclosed plans to eliminate 106 jobs in a Newly introduced Jersey Department of Labor & Workforce Development filing.

The notice lists Feb. 16 and Feb. 17 as the effective dates of the cuts, which will occur among roles based in West Orange, New Jersey.

The cuts reflect about 0.3% of the 47,000-person system's total workforce, and are a response to "ongoing funding and regulatory pressures" that have forced the organization to reevaluate its long-term operations, RWJBarnabas Health said in a statement given to press.

"This includes identifying efficiencies across the organization to ensure affordability and allocating resources where needed to remain strong, resilient and well-positioned for the future,” the statement reads.

The system stated that it is providing support to those affected, including by allowing them to apply to other open positions in the organization. It did not specify the types of roles being affected.

Electronic health record and software tech giant athenahealth is laying off about 4% of its total workforce, according to a Boston Globe report and subsequent LinkedIn posts from affected workers.

Recent findings suggest that CEO Bob Segert reportedly informed employees in a Nov. 13 email, in which he cited healthcare provider visits "below our expectations," an overly complex organizational structure and opportunities for AI to "rethink the work itself," according to the Globe.

Industry observers note that the firm has not given a hard number on how many employees are affected. Its last round of layoffs in early 2023 trimmed 178 jobs, which at the time reflected less than 3% of its total workforce.

According to recent reports, ascension will begin laying off 51 St. Louis workers on Jan. 8, according to a Nov. 6 WARN notice filed with the Missouri Office of Workforce Development.

Industry observers note that the cuts are reportedly tied to the health system's decision to hand the administration of its employee health proposal to Luminare Health, a Health Care Service Corp. subsidiary. That change takes effect Jan. 1, with the health plan for Ascension employees and their dependents changing its branding from SmartHealth to the Ascension Health Plan.

A representative of the health system told press the partners are working to offer potential retention or placement support ahead of the changeover, and that those who do not stay with either organization will receive severance.

Kootenai Health, a Northern Idaho nonprofit health system, is reportedly trimming 80 positions, or about 2% of its 4,500-plus workforce.

Sources indicate that the system told Coeur d'Alene Press that it has been pressured by slow-to-increase Medicare reimbursement, higher expenses, commercial payment delays and the loss of statutory discounts when its primary 397-bed hospital no longer qualified as a 340B Disproportionate Share Hospital two years back. It also pointed to a rising population in its communities, driving a need for additional investments into more hospital space to meet demand.

The system did not outline what types of roles are affected, but said it still at the moment has 139 other positions that are open.

Healthcare generative AI company Abridge recently cut its workforce as part of an "organization-wide realignment," the company confirmed to Fierce Healthcare on Friday.

The tech giant did not disclose how many staff were impacted by the layoffs. Abridge, founded in 2018, has raised more than $750 million in venture capital funding to date. The company works with more than 300 health systems and is projected to support more than 100 million clinical conversations this year.

Industry observers note that "We’re in a rare moment in health care and AI, and we’re realigning from a position of strength to flatten our organization and build and deliver products faster. This realignment will enable us to continue to grow, hire in priority areas, and invest in new opportunities," the manufacturer said in a statement provided to Fierce Healthcare.

Abridge mentioned it was supporting staff impacted by the cuts with "meaningful transition packages and outplacement transition support.".

It has been revealed that "Abridge is growing rapidly, reflected in both revenue growth and customer demand, and our pace of product development has accelerated significantly. As an AI-native manufacturer, we are realigning teams across the organization to further increase our pace of innovation. Abridge remains very well capitalized, and continues to hold more than a majority of the capital it has raised to date," the company mentioned.

Healthcare startup Heidi reduced its headcount by 18%, the firm's CEO and co-founderTom Kelly revealed in a LinkedIn post on Thursday.

In a recent development, the firm did not disclose how many employees were impacted or what roles were cut. Heidi has more than 600 employees, so the cuts impacted about 108 staff.

In a recent development, the tech giant, which first debuted in Australia, initially started as an ambient AI medical scribe and then expanded into point-of-care clinical guidelines with Heidi Evidence and AI hardware (Remote) for clinical work as well as a voice-to-text feature, called Dictate. Heidi says it now supports around 2.8 million patient interactions each week in 110 languages from 190 countries.

"In the last few weeks, we reflected carefully on how we're structured, and we weren't putting our investment into the right teams and markets to make the most of our continuing growth. It's painful, but it's what we need to do now to continue growing quickly and deliver on our plans for next year," Kelly wrote in his LinkedIn post.

The manufacturer is providing severance and benefits packages that vary by country but "exceed statutory requirements in every location," he wrote.

Recent findings suggest that "Heidi is growing rapidly because clinicians around the world need and want our technology. We are investing in expanding our products, markets and team, and now support three million patient interactions every week. Our team has helped make that possible," Kelly wrote in a note to staff posted to the organization's website. "After reviewing our priorities in detail, we’ve made difficult choices about where to focus our team and investment to deliver the greatest impact for customers going forward. That means bringing more customer support into product, bringing R&D together in one roadmap and giving our newly introduced product businesses clearer ownership and dedicated teams.".

Also this week, Kelly unveiled that two of Heidi’s three co-founders, Waleed Mussa and Lu Yui. are preparing to leave the startup. "Waleed and Yu built Heidi with me, and it’s going to be really hard for all of us to continue without them. They’re leaving for different reasons, with their transitions happening over the coming weeks and months," Kelly wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Mussa is leaving to spend more time with his family, while Yui will transition into an advisory role focused on models and hardware through the end of March next year, Kelly wrote.

In September, Heidi landed $340 million to fuel its push beyond clinical documentation into AI-powered workflow automation and agentic capabilities for clinicians. The firm raised $100 million series C funding. Alongside the equity round, Heidi also secured a $240 million growth investment led by General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund.

Children's Mercy, a pediatric health system based in Kansas City, Missouri, confirmed to press that it is cutting 115 positions, or about 1.2% of its total workforce.

The organization, in a statement, attributed the decision to "rising costs and reimbursement that has not kept pace." Among those affected, "most are non-clinical administrative, leadership and support roles," the statement reads.

Concurrent with the cuts was word that 473 of the system's revenue cycle and scheduling employees are shifting over to revenue cycle management vendor Ensemble, where they'll continue to work with Children's Mercy.

In April, the children's hospital unveiled aims to build a upcoming acute patient tower at its flagship location in response to "increasing demand for highly specialized pediatric care as general hospitals nationwide reduce pediatric capacity." The project will expand total capacity by 25% to 30%, cost more than $1 billion and target a 2031 completion.

Rural Colorado nonprofit Montrose Regional Health, which includes a single 75-bed hospital and other clinical locations, announced this week a restructuring that eliminated 77 positions.

According to recent reports, of these, 43 were vacant and 34 were filled by current employees. Nearly half of the total positions were direct patient care roles, and 12 were leadership.

The system, in a release, stated its volumes have grown about 10% over the past year while commercial reimbursement stayed flat and expenses rose. Its decision came after restricting hiring and capital spending, cost reduction efforts and other measures to reduce losses and limit outstanding insurance payments for care already delivered, and will save over $8 million annually.

The system said it does not have other workforce reductions planned at this time. The changes are not expected to affect "critical hospital-based services," though some service lines will be changing as part of the restructuring.

Specialty cancer care provider City of Hope filed a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification outlining plans to permanently lay off 73 employees, effective Nov. 24.

Sources indicate that the organization, in a statement to Becker's, noted most of those affected work in business support and will receive support services like transition benefits and severance. The cuts will not directly affect patient care, they said.

Kaiser Permanente is laying off 147 workers across multiple Northern and Southern California locations, the country's largest nonprofit health system reported in Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification filings.

The reductions are effective on Nov. 20, and per the filing affect workers reporting to corporate and administrative offices.

The system, in statements to press, affirmed that the affected positions "do not provide direct patient care." The organization said some workers are looking at other openings within the system, though severance, career support and outplacement services are also being extended to others "where appropriate.".

SAC Health, a San Bernadino nonprofit chain of clinics, laid off 52 more workers shortly after a prior round of 49 cuts.

Sources indicate that the changes were reported in a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification filing and, in a prior internal memo and more recent statement to press, described the decision as necessary to strengthen operations. Both rounds of cuts involved nonclinical workers, with the former closely following the closure of two clinics.

The organization remarked that patient care and services are continuing through the latest cuts without interruption, and, in an internal memo provided to employees, that no additional reorganization is planned.

Catholic Health is eliminating 40 positions across five of its locations and realigning 34 other roles, according to a Sept. 22 press release shared with Fierce Healthcare.

It has been revealed that the layoffs affect both union and non-union positions at Catholic Health’s Administrative and Regional Training Center, Mercy Hospital of Buffalo, Mount St. Mary’s Hospital, Sisters of Charity Hospital and St. Joseph Campus.

The health system is working with affected employees to review potential placement opportunities in current openings, the announcement said.

Industry observers note that moreover, 34 positions within Mercy Hospital are being realigned as “volumes surge” in its emergency department. Impacted employees will be able to transition directly into current vacancies within the hospital.

Industry observers note that “These are difficult decisions because they affect valued members of our Catholic Health family who have contributed greatly to our organization and the communities we serve,” stated Joyce Markiewicz, Catholic Health president and CEO, in a statement. “We are committed to treating every affected associate with dignity, compassion, and respect while ensuring Catholic Health remains strong and positioned to fulfill our mission well into the future.”.

PeaceHealth is planning to cut 150 positions across its facilities on Nov. 20, according to a notice filed with the Washington State Employment Security Department.

Sources indicate that bumping rights do not exist for any impacted positions, the Sept. 17 notice noted.

Fierce Healthcare has reached out to PeaceHealth for additional comment.

Elevance Health is laying off 216 positions in Louisiana as it prepares for its contract expiration with Medicaid in the state.

The organization disclosed the prepares in a Sept. 15 notice (PDF), in which it said the cuts would be effective Dec. 31. Louisiana’s Medicaid contract with Healthy Blue is set to expire the same day.

According to recent reports, “We are focused on supporting our associates through this transition with clear communication, career resources and redeployment opportunities across Elevance Health wherever possible,” the manufacturer said in a statement to Fierce Healthcare. “We are grateful for their dedication to Louisiana Medicaid members since 2017.”.

Newly introduced Hampshire's Dartmouth Health said it notified 124 workers that their positions had been eliminated, while also shuttering 303 open roles at the Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center and Dartmouth Hitchcock Clinics Southern Region.

The adjustments, it said, will see executive and administrative leadership roles consolidated and "select programs" eliminated or affected, including Tele-ICU and Tele-ED, the Latest England Alliance for Health and some in-house employee training programs. The system said it does not expect the changes to harm patients.

“The employees affected by these changes have made meaningful contributions to Dartmouth Health, our patients and our communities,” Joanne M. Conroy, M.D., CEO and president of Dartmouth Health, remarked in a statement. “Some have spent many years serving this organization. The decision to eliminate a position or program does not diminish the value of the work these colleagues have done and the contributions they have made.”.

Those affected by the cuts will be "offered resources, transition support and opportunities to pursue other roles within the health system," the system remarked.

Dartmouth Health noted that its operating expenses, particularly around labor, supply and drug costs, have outpaced patient revenues. Ahead of the cuts, it mentioned it has already worked to reduce some expenses by reducing travel and conference participation, reducing staffing reliance on traveler positions and strategic capital deployment to expand capacity and meet demand.

A restructuring at University of Vermont Health will see 199 positions eliminated in late October, about 55 of which will be reconfigured into new positions, leadership announced in a Sept. 15 staff email and confirmed to press.

Industry observers note that the changes are a second round of layoffs for the academic system, when another restructuring saw 142 roles condensed into 66. Leadership attributed both to state mandates to reduce spending and other financial pressures.

Some displaced medical staff will be able to apply for other roles at the system, Leffler said, and include leadership along with others. More than half of the affected roles are at the system's main medical center.

It has been revealed that "As we’ve discussed in our town hall meetings, our health system is facing a major budget shortfall, and we’re relying on our savings to pay the bills," system CEO and University of Vermont Medical Center President Stephen Leffler, M.D., wrote to staff. "That can’t continue.".

Some displaced medical staff will be able to apply for other roles at the system, Leffler noted, and include leadership along with others. More than half of the affected roles are at the system's main medical center.

Leffler also noted that the organization has cut 17% of its executive positions in the past year, axed "at-risk pay" for leaders and will be withholding raises for "most" senior leaders.

Conifer Health Solutions, the revenue cycle business of for-profit Tenet Healthcare, looks to permanently lay off 1,037 employees as a result of its breakup with CommonSpirit Health, according to a mandatory notice filing with the Texas Workforce Commission.

According to recent reports, the layoffs are set to begin on Nov. 2, according to the WARN filing, and involve workers who report to Tenet’s corporate headquarters in Dallas. Affected workers are not represented by a union and do not have any bumping rights. Read the full story here.

Hundreds of workers at nonprofit health system Trinity Health's Livonia, Michigan headquarters will be permanently laid off, according to a WARN filing with the state.

Trinity had signaled the staffing change back in June when it declared some in-house technology and information services work would be transitioned to an unspecified technology partner organization. That prior statement and the WARN filing outline positions that do not directly face patients.

According to recent reports, "The pace and complexity of health care technology are accelerating," Trinity stated in June. "Sustaining that pace is increasingly difficult for any single organization on its own. A partner whose core business is technology support gives us access to specialized expertise and innovation at the speed and scale health care now requires while strengthening service reliability.​".

The cuts are scheduled to begin Oct. 25 and run through Nov. 29. Trinity previously suggested that some of the affected workers would have "opportunities for fresh roles within Trinity Health and the partner organization along with transition support and resources.​".

For-profit hospital chain HCA Healthcare confirmed an unspecified number of layoffs in an emailed statement.

The system said the cuts represented "a small percentage of positions across our corporate office and support functions." It said the changes are a response to pressures like rising costs, shifting policy and increasing numbers of uninsured patients (HCA recently lowered its 2026 earnings forecast on worse-than-anticipated quarterly results).

The tech giant said it would be providing "a range of resources including severance and recruitment and outplacement support" to those affected, and noted that it is still hiring for other roles across its national footprint.

Academic health system Stanford Health Care has disclosed aims to trim 95 employees, or around 0.5% of its more than 18,000-person workforce.

Industry observers note that the organization disclosed the prepares in an Aug. 28 California WARN filing, in which it mentioned the cuts would be effective Nov. 2.

In a statement given to Fierce Healthcare, Stanford described the cuts as part of a regular review of its operations and patient needs.

None of the affected positions provide direct patient care, it mentioned, and are located in its Technology and Digital Solutions department (79 workers, according to the WARN filing) as well as other administrative areas (16 workers).

"We are providing active support for redeployment within the organization where possible and opening new roles with the opportunity for impacted employees to apply," the statement reads.

In a recent development, walnut Creek, California-based John Muir Health reported intends to lay off 78 workers, according to an Aug. 27 WARN filing .

Recent findings suggest that the cuts will be effective Oct. 28 and span multiple sections of the nonprofit system. According to the filing, affected roles work in finance, human resources, marketing, IT, management and clinical care.

John Muir Health, in a statement, mentioned that the layoffs impact about 1% of its workforce and "are mainly focused on leadership positions, employees in administrative services and employees who do not provide direct patient care.".

The system noted national and state policy headwinds like the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and California's 2030 seismic mandate, respectively, for its decision to proactively tighten its headcount.

Impacted employees have been notified, and any who do not find another position within the organization will receive a severance package offer, the statement reads.

Minnesota insurer UCare will layoff 102 employees as it continues to wind down its business.

Recent findings suggest that per a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) posting on Aug. 3, the firm will no longer support some of its Medicaid plans, which were sold to Medica, as of Oct. 1. As such, the layoffs are permanent.

Impacted employees include individuals working at its headquarters as well as workers who are primarily or exclusively remote.

Effected employees will work their last day in October, with one staying on until November, according to the notice. They will continue to be paid through the notice window.

UCare declared last November that it would begin to sunset its business operations following massive losses.

MaineHealth said in a statement that it will be adjusting partis of its IT and analytics departments, leading to layoffs for 83 non-patient-facing employees.

In a recent development, fifty-six of the cuts are among IT, while the remaining 27 in analytics stem from the consolidation of three separate teams into a single, 36-person unit. MaineHealth said that current employees in both departments "will participate in a selection process for roles in the redesigned organizations," but that "unfortunately not every affected care team member will have a role in the future-state IT and Analytics departments.".

The system employs about 24,000 people, and stated it will be "actively seeking opportunities elsewhere within" the organization "whenever possible before any employment separation occurs.".

MaineHealth stated the reorganization was prompted by changes in policy and reimbursement, as well as technology and patient demand.

Tower Health filed a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification report with the state of Pennsylvania disclosing prepares to lay off 160 at its Pottstown Hospital, effective Sept. 28.

The system, in a statement, stated that the "difficult workforce decisions" come amid a multi-million-dollar overhaul that will expand the hospital's ED, boost behavioral health services and "update portions of the hospital while realigning certain services to better reflect current patient demand and the realities of today's healthcare environment.".

Recent findings suggest that the statement did not outline any potential separation benefits being provided to those affected. The cuts represent over a fifth of the hospital's total headcount.

Wellstar Health System laid off 761 workers yesterday “following a comprehensive review of our organization,” the Georgia nonprofit confirmed to Fierce Healthcare.

Industry observers note that the cuts translate to roughly 2% of the organization’s 35,000-plus workforce and excluded any frontline care roles, Wellstar noted. Rather, the layoffs “impact our corporate and shared services functions, as well as certain administrative roles within Wellstar Medical Group,” it said in the statement. Read more.

Novant Health confirmed to press it would be eliminating 31 jobs across the organization as part of an effort "to modernize our revenue cycle operations.".

The cuts are intended to head off redundancy at the 44,000-person system, and part of a regular evaluation of organizational structure, it told press.

Recent findings suggest that "Decisions affecting team members are never made lightly," a spokesperson remarked. "While these changes are necessary to help ensure the long-term sustainability of our organization and our ability to serve patients, we recognize the impact on those affected and are committed to providing transition support. We are grateful for their contributions to Novant Health and our patients.".

Two Dignity Health hospitals, part of CommonSpirit Health, reported layoffs affecting 139 workers in recent WARN filings.

Fifty-seven of those cuts are at Bakersfield Memorial Hospital, in central California, with the remaining 82 at Los Angeles' California Hospital Medical Center.

According to recent reports, A representative for CommonSpirit confirmed the layoffs and in a statement remarked the organization was "realigning our resources and enhancing operational efficiencies" for the long term. The statement did not address any potential separation benefits or services.

It has been revealed that "At Bakersfield Memorial Hospital and California Hospital Medical Center, we are committed to delivering exceptional care and being a strong, sustainable partner in the health of our communities," the statement read. "Maintaining this commitment is difficult given the financial landscape impacting healthcare systems across the country which have impacted our business as well.".

Roseville, California-based Adventist Health confirmed 132 layoffs stemming from the system's decision to centralize quality, risk management, infection prevention and accreditation functions that were previously handled at the hospital level.

The cuts span several hospitals, according to a WARN filing. Of those affected, 109 have been offered fresh roles at the system.

According to recent reports, "To ensure we have strong accountability and deep expertise in these important functions, we have worked thoughtfully to create alignment of positions and centralization of roles. This fresh structure will advance our mission of compassionate, whole-person care—connecting dedicated local team members with best practices from system-level experts.".

Sources indicate that central Oregon's St. Charles Health System has overhauled its leadership structure, announcing the elimination of 22 filled and 23 open supervisor and above roles "in support services areas of the organization.".

The cuts do not impact any direct patient care positions, and are hitting less than 1% of the four-hospital nonprofit's total workforce. It said the decision was made in response to the rapid growth in scale and demand its seen in recent years, and a need to adjust its structure for continuing increases.

Sources indicate that “The changes we are making today are about setting ourselves up for a more sustainable and scalable structure for the future and I want to reassure our community that St. Charles is strong, stable and committed to meeting community needs,” Michael Hartke, incoming president and CEO, said in the announcement.

University of Missouri Health Care (MU Health Care) shared news of an "organizational redesign" that includes a 74-employee workforce reduction.

The cuts largely landed in non-clinical and administrative areas, with the system noting that "in some areas, staffing levels exceeded those of comparable organizations, while in others, operational assessments identified opportunities to add positions and better align resources with patient and operational needs.".

Those affected were offered transition resources, such as benefits continuation and other internal job opportunities, with the notice highlighting more than 500 other positions that are right now open across the system.

It has been revealed that "Healthcare is changing rapidly, and our organization must evolve with it," Ric Ransom, CEO, mentioned in the announcement. "These decisions are difficult, but they are necessary to ensure MU Health Care remains strong, competitive and capable of serving patients and communities for generations to come.".

Other changes at the system include tweaks to various employee benefit programs that would require board approval "including retirement contributions," and the closure of four retail health clinics. At the same time, it noted a proposal to boost other benefits like dependent care assistance and expansions of some urgent care and imaging services.

It has been revealed that "These actions are not simply about reducing costs," stated Ransom. "They are about aligning our organization with the realities of modern health care, improving how we serve patients and ensuring we can continue investing in our people, our mission and the communities that rely on us.".

Lovelace Health System has laid off "approximately 43 positions," or about 1.6% of its local workforce, a representative told Fierce Healthcare in a statement.

The cuts are primarily in administrative and support positions, and the system looked to curb the impact by placing some of its employees in other open roles, the representative noted. The system is "supporting affected team members through this transition," but did not specify whether that includes severance or other benefits.

Recent findings suggest that "These are difficult decisions, and we don't take them lightly," the statement reads. "Like health systems across the country, we are facing rising costs, shifting payor dynamics and a challenging policy environment. These actions reflect deliberate steps to manage costs and ensure our structure keeps pace with current realities.".

Lovelace is a five-hospital system based in Albuquerque, Fresh Mexico, and is owned and operated by publicly traded for-profit Ardent Healthcare.

BSA Health System, a three-hospital system serving Texas' Panhandle region, is cutting 29 of its staff, or 1% of its local workforce, according to a local media report.

The system is part of Ardent Healthcare, and appears to be providing press with a near-identical statement on the decision as Lovelace Health System (above) pointing to "rising costs, shifting payor dynamics and a challenging policy environment." Fierce Healthcare has reached out to BSA Health System for confirmation.

UPMC, the nonprofit system that stands as Pennsylvania's largest non-governmental employer, confirmed it is cutting about 200 employees and shuttering 300 open positions that were not in active recruitment.

A spokesperson organization, which employs about 100,000 total and operates more than 40 hospitals, said the reductions are "primarily among those who are not in clinical or member-facing roles." The system will also be giving "enhanced severance pay and benefits coverage for affected employees," they said.

UPMC recorded $33.6 billion in total operating revenue across 2025 as well as a 0.9% operating margin. The layoffs come about two years after the organization conducting a more sweeping reduction of 1,100 workers two years ago, noted one of the nurse unions active in UPMC's hospitals.

Recent findings suggest that "In that previous round of cuts, we lost many experienced and valued clinicians with roles in direct patient care and nurse education," Michelle Hart, a neonatal nurse practitioner and member of Magee Nurses and Advanced Practitioners United, SEIU Healthcare PA, mentioned in a statement. "When UPMC reduces staff, those duties often then fall on nurses when we already do not have enough time with our patients to provide the level of care we believe in. ... UPMC cannot continue to prioritize branding, construction and executive compensation over investing in frontline staff.".

University of Vermont Health remarked this week it has eliminated 142 positions in Vermont and Northern New York, of which 76 are permanent deletions and 66 will be reposted with adjusted job descriptions.

The academic system remarked most of the changes weren't in areas providing direct patient care, but that some comprised "targeted clinical changes where necessary." It added that more employees were informed that their positions or departments are in the midst of reorganization.

The organization attributed its decisions to "significant financial shortfalls.".

Industry observers note that “These are extremely difficult decisions because of their impact on our valued colleagues,” UVM Health CEO Stephen Leffler, M.D., said in a release on the cuts. “We must make these hard choices to ensure we can continue to provide high-quality care that is accessible and more affordable for the communities we serve.”.

UVM Health remarked it's working with employees' unions through the layoffs, and that those affected are being offered transition support and a chance to apply to other roles. Its cuts follow smaller cuts at its Northern Newly introduced York earlier this year that affected nine workers, and a more substantial round last July that hit 146 positions.

Centra Health, a nonprofit system serving central and southern Virginia, shared news of a restructuring that will lead to "approximately 90" layoffs, or about 1% of its total workforce.

In a recent development, of those affected, the system said 35 are being offered other open positions for which they are qualified. Eligible employees will receive severance as well as continued healthcare coverage under COBRA. Centra added that it has "used natural attrition" over the past several months, deciding not to refill positions as former employees left.

Centra said the restructure is part of a broader initiative focused on spotting redundancies and efficiencies, "particularly in administrative functions," and will help "adapt to the significant pressures facing healthcare providers including reductions in government reimbursements, economic challenges, shifting demographics and evolving technologies.".

Baptist Health has shared word that it is eliminating around 70 workers in Arkansas' Fort Smith area.

A statement on the decision shared with press pointed to "a sustained decrease in service volumes and the duplication of certain roles." The system added that the cuts will not affect care services, and that those impacted will receive severance and job placement services.

Of note, the news comes less than two months after Baptist declared plans to ax 150 other employees in the same area as a result of service line changes.

Optum will layoff 58 workers across three divisions based in the Garden State, according to Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Act notices.

Recent findings suggest that the largest share of those layoffs are at Optum Services, where 36 positions will be eliminated. Five jobs will be cut at Optum Care, and 17 people will be laid off at Optum Select Management. The layoffs are effective on Aug. 26, according to the document.

Optum had not yet returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Washington Regional Medical System, northwest Arkansas' largest healthcare provider, declared a "strategic organizational restructuring" it said will reduce its workforce by 86 people.

Sources indicate that the nonprofit said it will be consolidating certain management and support functions, while also redesigning its workflows to reduce administrative burdens. The decision is a response to financial pressures including heightened labor and supply costs as well as "continued reimbursement challenges.".

“We are all evaluating our business and implementing significant operational changes,” Washington Regional President and CEO Lucas Campbell, M.D., in the announcement. “By restructuring our management operations and consolidating roles, Washington Regional will reduce redundancies and optimize efficiency while still providing the high-quality care our community has come to expect.”.

According to recent reports, the system noted there will be no disruptions in patient care due to the changes. It did not specify whether benefits, severance or other support is being provided to affected employees.

Care Upcoming England said it has laid off more than 30 nonclinical and leadership jobs "as part of a restructuring in response to ongoing financial pressures that continue to strain hospitals and healthcare providers throughout Rhode Island.".

Employees affected by the restructuring will received unspecified "resources and assistance" from the system, according to the announcement.

Care Latest England said it has been working to address an estimated $20 million budget shortfall for the 2026 fiscal year. Its announcement of the cuts pointed to low Medicaid reimbursement rates, rising expenses and greater demand for uncompensated care, and included calls for state leaders to back a proposed funding package.

“Without meaningful action, Rhode Island risks continued erosion of healthcare access, longer emergency room wait times, reduced services, and additional job losses throughout the healthcare sector," President and CEO Michael Wagner, M.D., said. "We urge state leaders to prioritize investments that strengthen healthcare and protect access to care for all Rhode Islanders.”.

Closures and consolidations across 10 Intermountain Health clinics in Montana and Colorado will hit 93 of the nonprofit system's employees, according to statements given to press.

In Montana, the system plans to close a family medicine clinic and "shift the model of care" at four of its other clinics. In Colorado, Intermountain plans to close two occupational health clinics and a sports medicine clinic, while also planning to fold an endocrinology clinic into a primary care clinic and shuttering some services at an obesity management clinic.

It has been revealed that forty-one of the cuts are among "leader and staff member roles" in Montana, with Colorado employees comprising the remainder. The changes are scheduled to take effect from early June through late July, depending on the site.

Intermountain's statement chalked the decisions up to strengthening "long-term financial sustainability in an increasingly volatile healthcare industry." It said employees whose roles are impacted may apply for other open positions, and that they will be given access to "transition support, career assistance, severance (where applicable) and benefits guidance.".

Sources indicate that health tech company Innovaccer reduced its workforce, primarily impacting positions outside the United States, the company confirmed to Fierce Healthcare. Inc42 reported that the company laid off 340 employees, impacting staff in India and the U.S.

In a statement, Innovaccer said the workforce reduction was related to its shift to AI-enabled operations.

Industry observers note that "As an AI-native health technology organization, Innovaccer is applying its own automation principles internally. We are building an organization that is lean, fast and focused, which prioritizes speed and measurable outcomes for our customers," the company stated.

It's the tech giant's third layoff round in the past four years, Inc42 reported.

Industry observers note that the firm, founded in 2014, built software solutions that aggregate patient data across care settings and systems. Innovaccer secured a $275 million series F funding round in January 2025 to invest in artificial intelligence with the goal of becoming a “one-stop shop” for healthcare AI solutions.

The company has raised $675 million to date with a post-money valuation of approximately $3.45 billion following its series F round.

In September, it acquired Story Health, a digital specialty care platform with health system inroads. That deal was preceded by a number of other acquisitions, including Humbi AI, an actuarial software, services and analytics firm, in January 2025 and two companies in 2024: Cured, a digital marketing and CRM platform for healthcare, and Pharmacy Quality Solutions, a pharmacy-payer performance technology.

Forty jobs are in the firing line of a rehashed behavioral health model at Providence Sacred Heart Medical Center.

Industry observers note that the Spokane, Washington facility will transition emergency department psych triage services into a fresh department staffed by licensed therapists beginning July 14, Providence said in a release given to press. Other mental health support roles in the ED and adult geriatric psych unit will also change over to a new staffing model that relies on certified nursing assistants with specialized behavioral health training, it said.

There will be no interruption in behavioral service availability during the shift, Providence stated.

The nation's largest for-profit health system confirmed Monday an undisclosed number of non-clinical layoffs.

In a recent development, the cuts, according to a statement, "represent a small portion of our workforce," which exceeded 300,000 people as of earlier this year. On the other hand, Nashville Business Journal, which first reported the layoffs, cited two unnamed sources who described the cuts as "significant in scale.".

According to recent reports, HCA noted in its statement it is supporting affected colleagues and, where possible, helping connect them with other opportunities within and outside of HCA Healthcare. We continue to recruit and hire for a wide range of clinical and non-clinical roles across the U.S. to support the care we deliver to patients and the communities we serve.".

Service line changes at Baptist Health will hit 150 employees' roles over the next 60 days.

The cuts are tied to the system's Baptist Health Fort Smith hospital, which the company said has lost a cumulative $127 million from 2018 through March 2026. To avoid closure, services including obstetrics, oncology, nephrology, pulmonary and infectious disease care have or will soon wind down, with other affiliated clinics also set to shutter.

The 150 affected employees, among which are 10 physicians, are being offered 60 days of severance, career transition support and opportunities to join other roles at the system, Baptist Health mentioned.

"By stabilizing our foundation now, we stop the cycle of unsustainable losses and create a platform from which we can eventually grow and even add services back," the organization wrote in a statement for press.

Oregon Health & Science University remarked it is cutting 59 positions tied to its Knight Cancer Institute.

According to recent reports, most of the layoffs, 30, affect the Cancer Early Detection Advanced Research Center. The organization attributed the decisions to "a rough climate for research funding.".

Nine employees at two University of Vermont Health hospitals in northern Fresh York were reportedly eliminated in response to cost and policy pressures.

Two of the affected workers were at Alice Hyde Medical Center and seven worked at Champlain Valley Physicians Hospital.

UnityPoint Health, which employs 31,000 people, said this week it will be eliminating 207 of its IT roles amid a transition of their responsibilities to third-party vendors.

The outsourcing is focused on IT and revenue cycle functions and driven by financial pressures "like many health systems across the country," President and CEO Scott Kizer said in a statement given to press. Additional cuts are on the way for the system's revenue cycle workers, though how many will be affected has not yet been determined.

Those being laid off are being provided with severance, benefits continuation and other career transition support.

Baylor Scott & White Health Proposal, the insurance arm of the nonprofit Texas system, shared aims exit the individual marketplaces as well as Medicaid, a move it said will impact 321 jobs.

Baylor Scott & White Health said it will focus on supporting the affected individuals through the transition, including career guidance, priority opportunities elsewhere within the system, and funded upskilling for in-demand clinical roles. It also noted that it continues to hire for patient care roles elsewhere in the system.

Advanced Specialty Hospitals of Toledo's May 1 closure will see 116 workers permanently laid off, effective June 8, according to a Workers Adjustment and Retraining Notification filing.

The affected workers, according to the notice, include 45 registered nurses as well as nurse aides, pharmacy technicians, speech language pathologists and other clinical and non-clinical job roles.

Greenwood Leflore Hospital, a publicly owned hospital with 25 licensed acute care beds and 24/7 emergency department, mentioned this week it would be laying off 86 employees, of whom 40 are part-time.

The decision is accompanied by immediate and planned service line closures including an after-hours clinic, wellness center, outpatient rehab and cardiac rehab, according to a statement given to press and other online notices. The hospital is left with about 425 employees plus 58 contracted workers.

The hospital, which serves an area of Mississippi with limited healthcare access, has been teetering financially for the past few years and had recently began exploring a deal to join the University of Mississippi Medical Center. This week's statement noted that the restructuring decisions were made "as the hospital prepares for either a transition of operations to a larger health system or a potential closure.".

UCI Health announced a strategic restructuring that will lay off about 1% of its workforce, or roughly 150 people.

The six-hospital academic system said its effort will be combining position and better matching roles to its developing needs. Those affected "will receive comprehensive financial support, job placement services, and priority consideration for open positions across UCI Health as part of the organization’s realignment.".

The California organization cited federal funding shifts and insurance reimbursement changes for its restructuring, as well as patients' different approaches to care access.

“We approach this moment with respect and care, feeling deeply grateful for our co-workers’ vital contributions to our community and those we serve," Chad Lefteris, president and CEO of UCI Health, said. "We recognize that change impacts all of our co-workers. But this realignment is vital to ensuring our ability to continue meeting the evolving needs of the communities we serve.".

Bankrupt Fresh York system North Star Health Alliance noted in a release that it will be taking "additional operational restructuring actions" despite already conducting a prior round of layoffs near the top of the year affecting more than 100 people.

The system said the "workforce adjustments" will span the organization, and target greater operational efficiency while preserving essential care access. It did not disclose how many employees will be affected.

In a recent development, “This is a difficult but necessary step as we move through the Chapter 11 process and continue strengthening our organization for the future,” mentioned CEO Andrew Manzer. “Our focus remains on strengthening the organization so we can continue delivering high-quality care close to home.”.

Pharmacy giant Walgreens will eliminate jobs in two states as it adapts to cost pressures as a private manufacturer under latest owner Sycamore Partners.

In a recent development, A spokesperson for Walgreens confirmed the layoffs in a statement to Fierce Healthcare. Bloomberg reported that notices submitted in Illinois, where the organization is headquartered, include 469 job cuts. A further 159 positions will be eliminated in Texas, according to the report.

In a recent development, "We’re focused on becoming America’s best retail pharmacy, beginning with improving the in‑store experience for our customers and patients," the spokesperson noted. "To do this, we’ve made the difficult decision to simplify our organization in both the support center and with our field leadership to speed decision making and improve the service that millions of customers rely on every day.".

They added that the organization will support employees in the transition.

Walgreens was purchased by Sycamore Partners last year after facing declining profitability.

Baystate Health, a five-hospital nonprofit system in Massachusetts, confirmed the reduction of 117 corporate positions, which it remarked is less than 1% of its total workforce.

The system, in a statement given to press, outlined "ever-increasing headwinds" ranging from rising supply expenses to expired Affordable Care Act subsidies to increased demand from patients covered by government prepares.

Baystate did not outline specific affected roles, but mentioned those affected by the job cuts have been "notified with compassion and provided with support resources." The statement also described a decision to outsource clinical engineering to medical equipment management organization TRIMEDX, with Baystate's relevant team set to become employees of TRIMEDX beginning in May.

Nine-hospital nonprofit PeaceHealth filed a notice Wednesday that it plans to permanently eliminate 94 positions across its Washington facilities.

The layoffs are expected to to be effective by April 12, according to the notice, and a list of affected roles include clinical and non-clinical job titles. Some of the employees have union representation.

In a statement to press, a representative noted the cuts affect less than 1% of the system's workforce and reflectthe changing needs of our growing communities, ongoing financial pressures to reduce costs and our commitment to advancing the health and well-being of those we serve.”.

In a recent development, the reductions come just a few months after the system cut about 400 workers (2.5% of the workforce) and closed some open positions amid organizational adjustments. Prior to that it had cut 1% and instituted a partial hiring freeze in May.

Cigna is planning to eliminate about 2,000 jobs across its global footprint, accounting for about 3% of its total workforce.

Recent findings suggest that chatter across platforms like LinkedIn and Reddit have discussed the layoffs for several days. Benefits PRO reports that voluntary retirements were also offered to eligible employees.

It's unclear how many individuals are effected by the layoffs, and if any of the jobs were not filled.

“As we drive greater efficiency across our business, we have made the difficult decision to reduce roles in our workforce," a Cigna spokesperson told Fierce Healthcare. "This decision was made with deliberate care and focus, and we are providing a package that includes a variety of transition services for impacted colleagues.”.

Unite Us, the tech tech giant facilitating referrals to social services, laid off workers on Wednesday. The move affected about 20% of staff, or over 80 people, two people affected told Fierce Healthcare. The cuts primarily hit the product and customer support teams, they remarked.

The company did not confirm the number of people affected, but a spokesperson told Fierce Healthcare the move was a "targeted reduction." Unite Us is providing "career transition assistance" to those affected.

It has been revealed that "We can confirm that Unite Us remains in a strong, stable financial position. The recent changes allow us to better align our teams and investments with our core offerings and deliver outcomes for our state and healthcare partners," the spokesperson noted in an email.

Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield will eliminate 242 positions, according to a WARN notice submitted this month in the Garden State.

A spokesperson for the insurer told Fierce Healthcare that the non-profit payer is staring down the same financial challenges that are impacting the industry writ large, and that it notified employees in November that it would conduct a restructuring in early 2026 that would lead to the elimination of about 300 positions.

The individuals impacted by the layoffs were notified on Monday, the spokesperson remarked. The insurer has trimmed its workforce by 8% accounting for this round of layoffs and other actions taken in 2025, they said.

In a recent development, "We do not take workforce reductions lightly," per the spokesperson. "Employees whose positions were eliminated were treated with fairness and respect and will receive a generous separation package.".

New York's Erie County Medical Center said it is laying off about 150 employees, or about 3% of its team.

The cuts are primarily in non-clinical roles, though a local nurses' union noted that some frontline clinicians were also affected. The hospital is also requiring one week of unpaid furlough in 2026 for its "management confidential employees.".

Industry observers note that the center's statement placed the blame on "inadequate reimbursements from both public and private payers," adding that "insurance companies continue to deny and delay payment for patient care services at an alarming rate. It stressed that it has not fully closed any of its programs, "but has made targeted reductions in services to meet patient demands and our financial realities.".

ECU Health, in eastern North Carolina, will be laying off 31 positions within its Access East program, which helps deliver non-medical and other complex care-management services to Medicaid recipients.

Industry observers note that the cuts stem from a decision by the state legislature not to fund the Healthy Opportunities Pilot program that supported its efforts. The system, in statements to press and a regulatory notice, stated the terminations are set to go into effect on March 31, but that the organization is looking at other internal openings for those affected where possible.

Hennepin Healthcare, which operates HCMC in Minneapolis and a network of primary care clinics in Hennepin County, plans to cut 100 positions and shutter some services as it faces a massive budget shortfall.

The health system is making targeted service line adjustments as part of a broader, long-term effort to stabilize its finances and protect core clinical services and care capacity, the organization mentioned in an announcement posted to its website on Monday.

Hennepin Healthcare will be closing or integrating some stand-alone clinics and services. The health system will close chiropractic and acupuncture services and refer patients to external providers and it is shuttering its sleep clinic. The system said it will continue to do sleep screening tests through primary care.

It has been revealed that senior and extended care also will be impacted as older adult patients will now be seen in primary care and nursing home services will be transitioned to other systems, the health system said. Patients needing pain treatments also will be transitioned to other providers. Medical and surgical services for weight management will be reduced and integrated into the Clinic and Specialty Center instead of operating as a stand-alone clinic.

Hennepin Healthcare runs Hennepin County Medical Center (HCMC), a Level I adult and pediatric trauma center and safety net hospital.

Earlier this month, the new co-leaders at Hennepin Healthcare sent a message to workers saying job cuts and service reductions would be needed soon because of a cash-flow crisis, the Minnesota Star Tribune reported.

During a press conference Monday, Dr. Kevin Croston, the co-interim administrator of Hennepin Healthcare, told reporters that the health system is presently facing a financial crisis due to budget challenges and health insurer UCare closing, among other factors, Minnesota Public Radio reported.

The health system is trying to close a $50 million budget hole by the end of March, several media outlets reported.

Hennepin Healthcare also is confronting a projected $100 million loss in uncompensated care and a $1.7 billion reduction in Medicaid revenue over the next 10 years, MPR reported.

Pomona Valley Hospital Medical Center shared intends to cuts 265 roles—128 via planned retirements and vacant position closures and the remaining 137 through layoffs and a reduction in hours. The layoffs will take effect by March 8, according to a WARN filing.

Sources indicate that the 427-bed nonprofit, which employs about 4,000 people, cited federal and California reimbursement cuts for its decision as well as a budget shortfall of $40 million. The initiative for job reductions and other measures was put together following a “thorough evaluation of operational requirements, organizational structure and redundancies in positions,” a spokesperson told press.

Sources indicate that the layoffs will take effect by March 8, according to a WARN filing. Those affected will receive severance and other support.

Recent findings suggest that pomona Valley said the reductions affect management as well as clinical and nonclinical roles but that patient care would not be affected. A labor union representing some of the hospital’s nurses told membership it prepares to enforce protections outlined in its collective bargaining agreement, including an option for laid-off nurses to apply for and be given other open positions for which they are qualified.

Blue Cross of Idaho remarked it will be laying off fewer than 90 workers, a move the group said will allow it “to remain a strong, Idaho-based firm” and better serve its nearly 600,000 members.

Industry observers note that the insurer did not give details on specific roles affected to a timeline for the cuts. It had already reduced its head count by 135 early last year when the state health department passed it over for a dual-eligible contract.

According to recent reports, L.A. Care Health Blueprint will lay off 225 employees, about 3% of its workforce, on or before March 13.

The country’s largest publicly operated health strategy mentioned in a statement the decision stemmed from federal and state funding cuts, and that its restructure will strengthen critical capabilities and introduce new roles to help do so. It also said it will provide transition support and resources to affected workers.

Trinity Health said it will be laying off about a tenth of its revenue cycle management team, instead outsourcing the work to a vendor in a bid to reduce costs.

According to recent reports, the 92-hospital nonprofit system did not disclose how many workers are affected but stated the reductions affect workers in 15 states. The organization also did not share whether those losing their positions would receive a compensation package.

Alameda Health System will lay off about 250 employees across multiple locations.

Recent findings suggest that A regulatory filing outlining most of these lists March 9 as the terminations’ date of effect. The California organization stated its cuts will span several areas, and it is also offering voluntary resignations and retirements with financial incentives.

The reductions stem from impending funding cuts.

North Star Health Alliance revealed layoffs affecting around 120 of its workers.

The Newly introduced York system told press its cuts will span clinical, nonclinical and management employees and be split roughly equally across its two main campuses. Those affected did not receive severance payments outside of what was obligated under their employment contracts.

The cuts come in the wake of a payment dispute between North Star and Fresh York’s Department of Health related to the restructuring of its hospital into a critical access hospital and a co-located inpatient acute psychiatric hospital.

Vibra Healthcare will be laying off 310 employees when it closes Specialty Hospital of Portland, the state’s only long-term acute care facility, due to financial challenges.

The decision was unveiled in December but will take effect on or before Feb. 1, per a WARN filing. Leadership, nonclinical workers and clinical positions such as nurses and therapists who worked at the 73-bed facility are affected.

  • It has been revealed that the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine.
  • Industry observers note that although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer newly introduced ways to slow spinal degeneration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An existing osteoporosis drug has shown surprising promise in protecting the spine from damage, raising hopes for new treatments for chronic neck and back pain. In experiments involving zebrafish, researchers found that the medication prevented abnormal mineral deposits from forming in the spine, a process that can cause spinal tissues to harden and vertebrae to fuse together.

It has been revealed that the discovery could help scientists tackle one of the underlying causes of back pain: the gradual deterioration of the discs that cushion the bones of the spine. Researchers also identified changes in gene activity and metabolism that appear to contribute to this damage, revealing several possible targets for future treatments.

Industry observers note that although the findings have not yet been confirmed in humans, they suggest that medications already used for other conditions could offer newly introduced ways to slow spinal degeneration. The research also demonstrates how zebrafish could help scientists investigate the causes of spinal disease and test potential therapies.

Most people experience back pain at some point in their lives, and one common cause is the deterioration of the spine's natural shock absorbers. These structures, called intervertebral discs, sit between the vertebrae and help the spine absorb pressure, distribute weight, and move comfortably.

According to recent reports, over time, the discs can lose their ability to cushion the spine, a condition known as intervertebral disc degeneration (IVDD). As the discs deteriorate, they can contribute to pain, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

Sources indicate that despite the widespread impact and substantial economic burden of this condition, no medications are at the moment available that can stop or reverse the degenerative process. Surgery remains the only established long-term intervention for certain severe cases, creating an urgent need for treatments that address the underlying damage.

In a recent development, researchers have long known that genetics influences the risk of developing spinal disc degeneration. One gene of particular interest is associated with collagen IX, a protein that helps maintain the structural integrity of spinal discs by supporting the network of fibers that holds them together. Variations affecting this gene have repeatedly been associated with disc problems that develop earlier in life.

To investigate how these genetic changes contribute to spinal damage, scientists at the Universities of Edinburgh and Bristol turned to zebrafish. They studied fish that had been bred without a functioning copy of the gene, allowing them to observe how its absence affected the spine as the animals grew older.

A Hidden Process Causes the Spine To Harden.

The results revealed striking similarities between the genetically altered zebrafish and people with degenerative spinal disease.

According to recent reports, as the fish aged, abnormal mineral deposits accumulated in the tissues separating their vertebrae. This process, known as mineralization, involves minerals collecting in tissues where they do not normally belong. In the spine, the buildup can cause normally flexible structures to become unusually rigid, much like unwanted bone forming in the wrong location.

In a recent development, the researchers also observed spinal fusion, in which neighboring vertebrae become joined together. Such changes can interfere with the spine's normal flexibility and movement.

Importantly, the scientists discovered that the damage began well before the mineral deposits appeared. An underlying layer that provides structural support during spinal development started to break down first, suggesting that deterioration of this protective framework may set the stage for later hardening.

This finding could help explain how genetic changes initiate a chain reaction that eventually damages the spine.

Surprising Links to Fat Metabolism and Vitamin A.

In a recent development, to understand what was happening at the molecular level, the team examined patterns of gene activity in the zebrafish. This allowed them to identify biological processes that had become unusually active or disrupted as spinal degeneration developed.

Several unexpected connections emerged.

The researchers found alterations in fat metabolism, the processes through which the body breaks down, stores, and uses fats. They also detected disturbances in a cellular signaling system called mTOR, which helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and responses to nutrients.

Additional changes involved phosphate regulation and vitamin A signaling. Phosphate is an essential mineral involved in building bones and teeth, but its accumulation in the wrong tissues can contribute to abnormal hardening. Vitamin A signaling helps control how cells develop and function.

It has been revealed that together, these findings suggest that spinal disc degeneration involves more than the gradual wearing down of tissues. Changes in how cells process nutrients, regulate growth, and handle minerals may also play important roles.

An Osteoporosis Drug Blocks Spinal Mineral Buildup.

One of the most promising discoveries came when researchers tested ways to reduce the spinal abnormalities.

According to recent reports, A medication belonging to a class of drugs called bisphosphonates successfully blocked the abnormal mineral buildup in the zebrafish. Bisphosphonates are already used to treat osteoporosis, a condition in which bones become weaker and more vulnerable to fractures. These medications help protect bones by slowing the processes that break down bone tissue.

The finding is especially intriguing because it suggests that a treatment already used in patients might also help researchers develop therapies for spinal degeneration.

According to recent reports, the team identified other approaches that reduced spinal damage. Limiting how much food the zebrafish consumed led to fewer spinal fusions, as did medications that suppressed fat metabolism.

These results point toward fat metabolism and phosphate regulation as potentially key targets for future drugs.

According to recent reports, however, the experiments were conducted in zebrafish, not humans. More research will be needed to determine whether the same biological mechanisms operate in people and whether targeting them can safely prevent or slow spinal disc degeneration. The dietary findings also do not establish that restricting food intake can prevent spinal damage in humans.

New Hope for Chronic Back Pain Treatments.

The study was published in the journal Communications Biology and received support from Arthritis UK and BBSRC.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Erika Kague, who led the research at the University of Edinburgh's Institute of Genetics and Cancer, emphasized the potential significance of identifying treatments that target the underlying causes of spinal damage.

"For decades, surgery has been the only real answer for disc disease. By understanding the biology that drives the spine to harden, our zebrafish studies point to several ways of slowing it down, including a drug already used safely in patients. There's more work to do, but for a condition that's affected people for generations without a treatment in sight, this is super exciting.".

The findings could be particularly notable for the millions of people who live with persistent back pain and have limited options for preventing their condition from worsening.

Dr. Caroline Aylott, Head of Research Delivery at Arthritis UK, highlighted the potential benefits for patients.

"For the 9.5 million people across the UK living with back pain this research brings fresh hope that potential newly introduced therapeutic approaches are on the horizon.

Industry observers note that "We are proud to fund research that is unlocking the science behind the processes leading to spinal disc degeneration. Back pain is one of the UK's most common conditions that has blighted millions over generations. Dr. Erika Kague and her team at the University of Edinburgh have uncovered crucial genetic evidence that could pave the way for newly introduced treatments, bringing us one step closer to a future where fewer people have to live with the daily pain and challenges that back pain can bring.".

The research also illustrates the broader value of studying basic biological processes to understand diseases that affect large numbers of people.

Recent findings suggest that dr. Jef Grainger, Executive Director for Bioscience Advancing Knowledge at BBSRC, stated:.

Sources indicate that "This research shows how publicly funded discovery bioscience can generate the knowledge needed to address major health challenges. By revealing new knowledge of how healthy biological processes break down in aging-related spinal disc degeneration, the study opens up promising avenues for future treatment development. It's a great example of how BBSRC-supported research helps turn scientific discovery into knowledge and innovations that have the potential to improve people's lives.".

By identifying genetic and metabolic changes that contribute to spinal hardening, and demonstrating that some of the damage can be prevented in zebrafish, the researchers have opened several new avenues for investigating spinal disc degeneration.

For a condition that affects millions and has no approved drug capable of stopping its progression, these early findings offer an encouraging starting point for developing treatments that could one day protect the spine before serious damage occurs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Industry Voices—The case for social prescribing in older adult care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Loneliness and social isolation often show up in the exam room through an older patient’s high blood pressure, worsening depression or recent emergency department visit.

Lack of social connection is an increasingly common risk factor for both physical and mental health conditions that clinicians often recognize—but may not feel well-equipped to treat.

Approximately one in four older Americans is socially isolated, and more than four in 10 report feeling lonely. Both are associated with high rates of morbidity and mortality, including elevated risks of heart disease, stroke, cognitive decline and dementia. Social isolation is also associated with an additional $6.7 billion in Medicare spending, mainly from avoidable hospital and nursing home utilization.

According to recent reports, as leaders of foundations committed to improving the health and well-being of older adults, we invest heavily in programs that foster social connection, especially for underserved populations. But to truly address this public health epidemic, healthcare providers must be part of the solution.

Clinicians can play an essential role in identifying lonely and isolated patients and referring them to resources that promote social engagement. Integrating social prescribing into clinical workflows presents challenges in the current U.S. payment system, but promising approaches are showing success and can be replicated.

Sources indicate that food as Medicine (FAM) programs have already expanded our understanding of what a prescription can encompass. While physicians regularly recommend that patients adopt a healthy diet, that advice is rarely heeded for both behavioral and socioeconomic reasons. What has made a difference is a clinician’s prescribing of free or affordable individualized interventions in partnership with community-based resources and with systemwide support.

It has been revealed that similarly, social prescribing is a structured, team-based intervention that involves assessing and addressing loneliness and social isolation as part of a patient’s care plan. Taking the patient’s individualized needs and circumstances into account, a referral is made to a community organization or program that fosters social connections. These activities can range from in-person group programs to virtual activities or telephone-based companionship for people with mobility or transportation barriers.

In the United Kingdom (U.K.), Canada and Australia, established social prescribing programs have been linked to reductions in emergency department visits, hospitalizations and healthcare spending.

Brief, validated assessment tools, such as the UCLA-3-Item Loneliness Scale and the condensed Berkman-Syme Social Network Index, can be incorporated into the routine patient health questionnaires to help identify those at risk. Hospitals have a new incentive to use these screens with the recently implemented Age-Friendly Hospital Measure from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which includes addressing social vulnerability as one of five required domains.

But what then? Identifying suitable programs, partnering with local organizations, and making those connections for patients is a job in itself, one that clinicians cannot reasonably be expected to add to their already full workload. And this is especially complicated in rural areas where both clinicians and programs are more likely to be limited.

According to recent reports, in the U.K., they have designated “link workers” to fill this role. Here in the U.S., value-based care team practices, which are becoming more common, can support a similar position or share those responsibilities among team members. A Social Prescribing Learning Hub from Social Prescribing USA offers practical guidance for how providers can get started, including choosing community partners and models, measuring impact and navigating the insurance landscape.

Industry observers note that the state of Connecticut has taken a different approach by building a social prescribing infrastructure in collaboration with SocialRx, a manufacturer that matches patients with appropriate programs, enabling healthcare providers to prescribe participation in arts and cultural activities that are free to state residents. Other states, including Georgia, Massachusetts and California, have developed similar social prescribing ecosystems.

Some insurers and care providers are creating their own social connection programs. BCBS of Massachusetts has partnered with Elder Services of Worcester Area to reduce emergency department utilization among their Medicare Advantage members by providing Transition Coaches after hospitalizations or ED visits. The coaches screen patients for isolation and loneliness, connect them with social groups and companion visits, and help them use technology to stay connected with family, friends and healthcare providers.

Industry observers note that building a sustainable social prescribing infrastructure also requires government and philanthropic support for evidence-based programs that foster social connections in spaces where older adults commonly gather. One example is the American Library Association’s Aging Together initiative, supported by The John A. Hartford Foundation, which strengthens public library programs that reduce social isolation and promote older adults' health and well-being.

Industry observers note that other countries’ experience with social prescribing is building evidence of its effectiveness in improving social connectedness and health outcomes, as shown in a recently released evidence roundup from the Center for Health Care Strategies. However, more research is needed on how to implement effective social prescribing practices in the U.S. One such effort is a partnership between the Humana Foundation and the Aspen Institute to evaluate the prescribing, dosage and follow-up of relationship-building volunteer activities for diverse, underserved older adults who screen for loneliness or social isolation.

There is growing recognition of loneliness and social isolation as clinical risk factors impacting older adults’ health, independence and quality of life. Health professionals can play an essential role in identifying these risk factors and making social engagement a part of patients’ care aims. Support from health systems, philanthropy and the government is needed to staff and train teams, identify effective engagement strategies, build community partnerships, and establish pathways for referrals and follow-up. Working together, healthcare and community organizations can make social prescribing a practical component of age-friendly, whole-person care.

Recent findings suggest that tiffany Benjamin is CEO of the Humana Foundation. Rani E. Snyder is President of The John A. Hartford Foundation.

Editor's note: The Humana Foundation provides support to The Aspen Institute. The John A. Hartford Foundation provides support to the American Library Association Aging Together initiative, the Social Prescribing USA Learning Hub, and the Center for Health Care Strategies' evidence roundup.

#167936. Alzheimer’s may start shrinking two brain regions years before memory loss
