Breaking: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1050 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most important stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery.
  • Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time.
  • Sources indicate that REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most important stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery. Developed by researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin, the device uses gentle ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, helping people enter REM sleep sooner and spend more time in this restorative stage.

Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time. This allows researchers to influence brain regions involved in sleep while simultaneously tracking how the brain responds.

Sources indicate that REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. It also plays an important role in processing emotions, consolidating memories, and adapting to stress. Disturbances in this stage of sleep have been associated with several mental health conditions, making it an important target for newly introduced treatments.

Industry observers note that "This is the first time we've been able to noninvasively target deep brain regions involved in REM sleep, while simultaneously monitoring brain activity," noted Kai Wing "Kevin" Tang, a recent UT biomedical engineering Ph.D. graduate who led the research effort.

Sources indicate that "Our skin-attached NEUSLeeP patch opens up newly introduced possibilities for understanding sleep and treating sleep disorders in home settings," added Huiliang "Evan" Wang, assistant professor in the Cockrell School of Engineering's Department of Biomedical Engineering. Wang supervised Tang's research and served as the principal investigator (PI) overseeing the project.

Sleep Patch Helps People Reach REM Sleep 43 Minutes Faster.

The early results suggest that the technology can make a measurable difference in how people experience REM sleep.

In a study involving 28 participants, published in Nature Communications, people using the patch entered REM sleep an average of 43 minutes sooner and spent approximately 16 additional minutes in that stage.

These improvements were observed in both healthy sleepers and participants experiencing certain sleep difficulties. The volunteers also reported that the patch was comfortable to wear, with minimal adverse effects.

Unlike medications that affect the body more broadly, NEUSLeeP is designed to deliver stimulation to specific brain regions involved in sleep regulation. It uses ultrasound, a form of sound energy with frequencies beyond human hearing, to reach areas beneath the surface of the brain without requiring an invasive procedure.

The findings are encouraging, although the relatively small study means that larger trials will be needed to determine how consistently the technology works and whether its benefits persist over time.

Potential Benefits for Stress and Emotional Health.

The researchers also found evidence that the patch's effects may extend beyond increasing REM sleep.

In a recent development, among healthy participants, ultrasound stimulation improved heart rate variability, a measure of the natural differences in time between consecutive heartbeats. This measurement provides insight into how the body's nervous system responds to stress and adjusts to changing conditions.

In a recent development, brain imaging revealed changes in neural circuits involved in emotional processing. Together, these findings suggest that improving REM sleep through targeted stimulation could potentially support emotional regulation and the ability to cope with stress.

According to recent reports, "REM sleep is not just about dreaming -- it's about emotional reset and stress adaptation," explained Gregory Fonzo, assistant professor in the Dell Medical School's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and one of the project's co-PIs. "By enhancing REM, we may help people better cope with stress and improve their overall well-being.".

These possibilities are especially interesting because REM sleep disturbances have been linked to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Current approaches to sleep problems often involve medication or behavioral therapy. Although these treatments can be effective, medications may produce unwanted side effects, and existing approaches do not always directly address the biological processes responsible for disrupted REM sleep.

According to recent reports, A device capable of influencing those processes without drugs or surgery could therefore offer an additional treatment option. However, the researchers have not yet established whether NEUSLeeP can improve symptoms of mental health disorders.

A New Direction for Treating Insomnia and PTSD.

Building on the initial findings, the research team intends to conduct larger clinical trials to confirm the patch's effects and investigate its potential use in people with PTSD, depression, and chronic insomnia.

It has been revealed that beyond treating sleep disorders, the technology could eventually support sleep monitoring at home and provide scientists with a fresh way to study how deep brain regions influence sleep. Researchers also envision personalized therapies that could be adjusted to individual sleep patterns and needs.

"Our vision is a future where patients with mental health disorders can optimize their sleep with a noninvasive and safe treatment," noted Vincent Mysliwiec, M.D., a professor at UT Health San Antonio, a leading expert in sleep disorders, and another co-PI on the project. "This technology could help millions of people get the restorative sleep they need.".

Recent findings suggest that the team is already taking steps toward making NEUSLeeP available beyond the research setting. Working with the university's commercialization unit, Discovery to Impact, the researchers are exploring how to bring the device to market and have filed a patent application covering the technology.

If future studies confirm the early results, this wearable ultrasound patch could become a valuable upcoming tool for improving REM sleep and potentially addressing conditions associated with poor sleep.

It has been revealed that other members of the research team include William D. Moscoso-Barrera, Mengxia Yu, Mengmeng Yao, Jinmo Jeong, Ilya Pyatnitskiy, Anakaren Romero Lozano, Jiachen Wang, Ju-Chun Hsieh, Tony Sungjin Chae, Daniel Song, Julieta Garcia, Rithvik Mittapalli, and Adam Bush of the Department of Biomedical Engineering; Benjamin Baird of the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Psychology; and Wynn Legon of Virginia Tech's Fralin Biomedical Research Institute.

Materials provided by University of Texas at Austin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#167912. Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (792 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Own, don’t rent: Why agentic AI is pulling cloud computing back on-prem

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it.
  • That shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure.
  • “Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:46 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Agentic AI is reviving an argument over renting versus owning compute, and the model plane — the layer that decides where AI models run — sits at the center of it. Open-source efforts such as Upbound Inc.’s Modelplane route inference across clouds, but many enterprises want the models on hardware they control.

That shift favors companies that built early for on-premises cloud infrastructure. Oxide Computer Co., which raised $445 million in October to expand rack production, built its business on the idea that enterprises at scale will want to own their computers, according to Bryan Cantrill (pictured), co-founder and chief technology officer at Oxide.

“Cloud computing is great, but the model shouldn’t be exclusively to rent it. You get to a certain scale, as it turns out, you want to own your own computer,” Cantrill remarked.

In a recent development, cantrill spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed renting versus owning compute, why agentic workloads are moving on-prem and multi-tenancy for isolating those workloads.

Industry observers note that agentic workloads are driving an explosion in compute demand, and much of it is CPU-heavy work that enterprises would rather own than rent. Economics remains the main reason to bring it in-house, but where models live is a close second, Cantrill explained. That makes the model plane as much a data governance decision as an infrastructure one.

“There is a real enterprise drive towards open-weight models, and I think you’re going to see more and more of that as people want to run the models on-prem and allow their data to not actually leave,” Cantrill said.

Security is the other half. Oxide stripped the UEFI BIOS and baseboard management controller out of its rack to shrink the attack surface, and built public cloud-grade multi-tenancy in from the start. Those early design choices give enterprises a perimeter for isolating agentic workloads, according to Cantrill.

Industry observers note that “I think multi-tenancy means you’ve got potentially adversarial tenants that are going to be on the same resource,” Cantrill noted. “They’re going to be sharing the same computer, sharing the same network, and they need to do that … without violating the confidentiality, without breaching one another.”.

Recent findings suggest that the same racks can take on legacy virtualization workloads from customers unhappy with pricing changes at Broadcom Inc.’s VMware business. That lets enterprises run old and fresh applications on one general-purpose platform, Cantrill noted.

According to recent reports, “You want all that flexibility that you get from elastic compute, but you need it for economic reasons, security reasons, latency reasons,” Cantrill noted of the case for on-premises cloud computing. “You need it in your own data center. You want to control your fate.”.

Unpacking the implications from CMS' latest proposed Medicare Advantage changes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Late last week, the Trump administration released a proposed rule that includes a slew of technical changes in Medicare Advantage for 2028, citing enhanced competition as a key goal.
  • Analysts dove into the beefy regulation and projected that changes to MA's star ratings program would likely cull more than $100 billion in federal spending over the next decade.
  • Per a note from Leerink Partners, estimates from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services suggest that the changes would cut federal spending by $11.5 billion in 2031 and $107 billion through 2037.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Unpacking the implications from CMS' latest proposed Medicare Advantage changes" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Late last week, the Trump administration released a proposed rule that includes a slew of technical changes in Medicare Advantage for 2028, citing enhanced competition as a key goal.

Analysts dove into the beefy regulation and projected that changes to MA's star ratings program would likely cull more than $100 billion in federal spending over the next decade.

Per a note from Leerink Partners, estimates from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services suggest that the changes would cut federal spending by $11.5 billion in 2031 and $107 billion through 2037.

The Leerink analysts estimate that about 58% of Medicare Advantage contracts would see lower scores using the newly proposed methodology, with about 20% of contracts losing quality bonus payments, which are tied to star ratings performance.

In the rule, CMS proposed moving to a set of 15 measures to determine the star ratings scores, which are focused on member experience and outcomes. The proposed rule would also eliminate the Reward Factor, and in tandem, these changes "would remove a cushion for contracts sitting at the critical QBP threshold, while concentrating performance across fewer measures," according to the Leerink report.

The analysts said that the potential impact of these proposals "reminds us just how many intends have been living at 4 stars for years with the hugely key Reward Factor.".

In a recent development, the report estimates that the changes to the star ratings, if finalized, would have an uneven impact on insurers. For example, Humana would see the number of contracts earning four or more stars decline from 95% to 82.9%. Clover Health, meanwhile, would likely maintain 100% of its contracts, earning at least four stars.

Sources indicate that unitedHealthcare, by comparison, could see a drop from having 67.9% of its contracts in prepares with at least four stars in 2027 to just 8.8% under the upcoming methodology. For Aetna, the Leerink analysts project a decrease from 70% to 0%.

Sources indicate that given the scale of the changes, the Leerink analysts write that the rule sets the stage for a significant overhaul of the policies and rules that govern Medicare Advantage. The proposal is "almost overwhelming in size, scope and the impact on the industry.".

Molly Turco, a policy analyst at TD Cowen, wrote in a note Monday that the proposed rule "is more significant than expected, in both revenue impact and scope and touches most core aspects of MA.".

"It appears CMS aimed to reform long-standing concerns, especially Stars, in a way that takes money out of the program, while also loosening regulation on things like agents/brokers, seamless enrollment, network adequacy, etc. to help the program grow," Turco wrote. "However, we think these growth/deregulation policies are unlikely to offset the headwinds for MA.".

She noted that while most of the most painful changes wouldn't impact prepares until 2031 at the earliest; the delay does suggest CMS may be comfortable including more significant short-term changes to risk adjustment in the forthcoming 2028 Advance Notice, which is expected in January.

Ryan Langston, an equity research analyst at TD Cowen, wrote in the note that the proposed rule would likely be net negative for insurers with large, multi-state contracts and more people enrolled with intends earning at least four stars.

The delayed timeline of at least four years does grant aims time to adapt, Langston wrote, but the financial impacts would likely force benefit changes. The proposed rule could also spook investors concerned about what's included in the 2028 rate notice, he said.

"The combination of a smaller measure set, elimination of reward factors and reduced improvement measure protection likely lower Star ratings across the industry and force looks to mitigate lost revenue via benefit revisions," Langston wrote.

The Leerink analysts wrote that health intends are almost certain to fight the regulation. Lawsuits have become commonplace in the stars space, with multiple payers suing the feds over the most recent round of scores.

Recent findings suggest that "We believe a lot of what has been proposed will change and/or not be implemented at all," they wrote. "Expect industry litigation.".

#167910. Breaking: Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1498 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1498 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits.
  • In a recent development, researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease.
  • The results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

In a recent development, researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

The results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the latest findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk.

According to recent reports, to investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

It has been revealed that participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

This distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

People consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

Industry observers note that moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks.

The clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

However, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

The contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

It has been revealed that these percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

In a recent development, "Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen said. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk.".

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

Wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen stated.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health.

Recent findings suggest that to make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several vital limitations.

Recent findings suggest that because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

In a recent development, alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

Another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

The researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

In a recent development, nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an important distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

Industry observers note that for now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Filmmaker Steven Spielberg has sold the sprawling Los Angeles ranch where he housed his horses for $22.3 million—just two months after listing the palatial estate.

Spielberg, 79, and his wife, Kate Capshaw, 72, purchased the property in 1999 through their corporate entity, Texas Tart, for $5.75 million.

In a recent development, they listed the massive compound in September for $30 million. Then, in late October, the home disappeared from the market with no indication why.

Now, Realtor.com® can exclusively reveal that the property has traded hands, selling for $22.3 million—at a nearly $8 million discount.

When they purchased the home, the Hollywood mogul and actress unveiled ambitious plans to dramatically overhaul the estate with a 27,000-square-foot, five-story riding facility featuring a domed roof and underground horse stables.

Spielberg's vision reportedly included more than $7 million in renovations, as well as aims to construct a 2,400-square-foot guesthouse and a three-story guardhouse.

Sources indicate that however, neighbors objected to the scale of the project. While the Oscar-winning director reportedly planned to present revised ideas to his neighbors, the elaborate project ultimately never came to fruition. Meanwhile, he did update the estate into the magnificent abode it is today.

Sources indicate that the property was held by Spielberg and Capshaw for nearly three decades. Last month, the couple decided to finally part ways with the equestrian retreat, listing it for $29.9 million with Sandro Dazzan of The Agency.

Known as Dogwood, the seven-bedroom, 9.5-bathroom estate sits on 2.8 acres in the secluded Sullivan Canyon. It offers an impressive array of equestrian amenities alongside its luxurious living spaces.

"Nestled in the ultra-private Sullivan Canyon, Dogwood is Los Angeles' premiere equestrian ranch—a rare masterpiece designed by renowned architect Michael Kovac with interiors by Michael Smith and landscape design by Christine London," the listing stated.

Spanning two parcels, the property combines a sophisticated country-inspired aesthetic with extensive facilities designed for horses, entertaining, and guests.

Inside the main residence, rich walnut floors and wood-covered ceilings create a warm atmosphere, while expansive windows bring in plenty of natural light.

The spacious living room offers multiple seating areas anchored by dual fireplaces, creating an inviting space for relaxing and entertaining.

That rustic aesthetic continues into the chef's kitchen, which features extensive wood cabinetry, an oversized center island, high-end appliances, and an eat-in dining nook.

"The chef's kitchen with eat-in dining nook and wood-burning fireplace connects to a cozy family room and IPE-clad terrace overlooking a tranquil reflection pond," the listing noted.

Upstairs, the primary suite offers a peaceful retreat complete with a wood-burning fireplace and access to a private covered terrace.

The outdoor space boasts yet another fireplace along with sweeping city and canyon views, according to the listing.

Elsewhere inside the home is a media room that can double as a game room, as well as a wine cellar.

But the property's most impressive features are arguably those designed for its four-legged residents.

Across from the main entertaining spaces sits a six-stall barn complete with an executive office, staff quarters, three grooming stations, a feed kitchen, and storage.

The equestrian facility is topped off by a sprawling 20,000-square-foot riding arena with an observation deck and mirrored wall, which the listing notes is suitable for both dressage and jumping.

The estate's lower parcel expands the compound with a stylish one-bedroom guesthouse equipped with its own kitchen, rooftop deck, and basement office and storage spaces.

There is also a second four-stall barn, a 5,400-square-foot turnout area, a private gate, and parking for more than 10 vehicles.

Sources indicate that both parcels are supported by a security command post and generators. The ranch is surrounded by lush landscaping, while a tranquil reflection pond adds to its secluded, countryside atmosphere—despite the estate's location in the heart of Los Angeles.

With this $29.9 million listing, Spielberg and Capshaw are closing a decades-long chapter. Even without having resided in this property, the couple aren't short on lavish abodes to call home.

Their main residence is a stunning Pacific Palisades abode, which has served as their home since 1985.

The property spans 20,000 square feet and boasts a media room, a 14,000-gallon aquarium, and several other lavish amenities.

Over in Malibu, they own a beachfront abode, which is made up of two parcels.

They purchased the first parcel in 1989 for $3.3 million and the second in 2000 for $3.2 million.

The home is situated on a 1.44-acre lot and boasts 144 feet of ocean frontage.

They also hold the keys to a dwelling in New York, which they purchased in 1983.

The couple snapped up the 6-acre estate and enlisted architect Charles Gwathmey to overhaul the abode.

Over the years, he added horse stables and a lavish guesthouse.

In 2008, he expanded the property by picking up a 3.2-acre pond in the front of the home for $20 million.

Also on the East Coast, the couple own a 6,000-square-foot apartment building in Manhattan.

HHS: Medicaid state-directed payment savings 'primarily' stem from slowing growth" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Rural hospitals claim a relatively small portion of the state-directed payments being squeezed in coming years by 2025’s H.R. 1, with much of the legislation’s projected spending reductions the result of holding funds for those hospitals from growing beyond fiscal year 2025 levels, Department of Health and Human Services policy heads wrote in a upcoming report.

The analysis, released Monday, paints a softer picture of the rate limits Republicans imposed on a supplemental Medicaid payment stream in last year’s broad budget reconciliation law, also referred to as the One Major Beautiful Bill Act or the Working Families Tax Cut Legislation.

Hospitals and other healthcare industry groups, as well as advocates and Democrats, have said the law’s billions in projected savings—from state-directed payment changes as well as other policy areas like Medicaid work requirements—are likely to devastate providers already operating at thin or negative margins.

Sources indicate that specifically, the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation (ASPE)’s analysis revealed that an estimated 7.8% of Medicaid state-directed payments reached rural hospitals in FY2025, or $11.5 billion out of $148.3 billion. That rate is slightly above rural hospitals’ 7% share of total Medicaid hospital spending for that same fiscal year, as estimated by the CMS Office of the Actuary.

Scaling from that baseline in line with H.R. 1’s multi-year payment rate phasedown, with some cumulative adjustments, demonstrated that total nominal cumulative spending on rural state-directed payments would decline by 42.9%, or $81.6 billion, from 2026 through 2035 under the bill. This rate is again slightly higher than the CMS Office of the Actuary’s 40.8% estimate for all affected hospitals, which ASPE remarked is the result of the higher average dollar weighted payment rates rural hospitals right now receive, “which means that rural providers have more room to reduce rates to meet the new limits of 100% to 110% of Medicare.”.

In a recent development, the ASPE report’s bottom line, however, is that $75.2 billion of the $81.6 billion reduction rural hospitals face, or 92.1%, reflects projected increases over the FY2025 baseline of $11.5 billion. The remainder, about 7.9% of the projected change, is a reduction below FY2025’s estimated state-directed payments to rural hospitals.

HHS, in a release highlighting the report’s findings, remarked that the language used in government reports describing the full $81.6 billion 10-year spending reduction as “savings” misses the government’s primary goal of capping future growth.

“Counting every dollar of projected savings as a cut below existing funding gives the public the wrong picture. Most of these savings are not reductions below what the program spent in 2025,” HHS Chief Economist and Chief Regulatory Officer Casey Mulligan, who was one of the report’s coauthors, noted in the release. “They reflect future spending increases that will no longer occur. Our analysis makes that distinction clear.”.

Sources indicate that H.R. 1’s multi-year scale down in state-directed payment rates is set to begin in 2028, and are expected to slash some hard-hit states’ Medicaid spending by up to a quarter of their total annual Medicaid spending, per one analysis. Hospitals have broadly criticized the policy changes while spending much of this year adjusting their operations to contend with the future limits supplemental revenue, expectations of increased uncompensated care costs and year-to-year expense pressures like wage and supply inflation.

Additionally, CMS earlier this year proposed state directed payment caps substantially more extensive than what was outlined in H.R. 1 and used as the basis for Monday’s ASPE report. That proposal would extend rate limits beyond the bill’s four outlined service areas (inpatient hospital services, outpatient hospital services, nursing facility services and qualified practitioner services at an academic medical center) to “all [state-directed payments]s for all services in all states.” Hospital groups have flatly opposed the proposal, which more than triples the 10-year estimated savings.

Industry observers note that lawmakers last year, when seeking votes, blunted H.R. 1's funding reductions for rural hospitals by inserting a five-year, $50 billion rural health fund into the legislation. Those funds have come with usage restrictions for states and providers, with critics also noting transparency concerns and the fund's relatively small scale compared to the bill's total projected impact on hospitals.

Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering crucial questions about its effects on mental health.
  • Industry observers note that published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition.
  • The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering crucial questions about its effects on mental health. A major latest study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Industry observers note that published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

In a recent development, "What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an crucial mental health concern that deserves attention.".

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link.

The connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults showed particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

The consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

It has been revealed that yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

According to recent reports, "Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood.".

Why Cannabis Use Disorder Matters.

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

In a recent development, the study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is notable because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

Industry observers note that the findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening.

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

In a recent development, "Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," said Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support.".

The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an notable role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence has turned data infrastructure from a back-office purchase into the bottleneck that decides how fast GPUs pay off.
  • The storage industry’s longtime performance specialist sees that shift as its opening.
  • Recent findings suggest that “When you look at the data layer, performance in the data layer drives value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:27 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Artificial intelligence has turned data infrastructure from a back-office purchase into the bottleneck that decides how fast GPUs pay off. As hyperscalers, neoclouds and enterprises race to expand their data layers, the way that infrastructure gets bought is changing just as fast.

The storage industry’s longtime performance specialist sees that shift as its opening. DataDirect Networks Inc. built its reputation on scale and speed, and those traits now carry more weight in AI infrastructure, according to Kevin Delane (pictured), president and chief revenue officer of DDN.

Recent findings suggest that “When you look at the data layer, performance in the data layer drives value. So yes, it has to be simple, it has to be reliable. Those are table stakes, but performance drives business value,” Delane said.

Delane spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI infrastructure sales cycles have grown more complex and faster, DDN’s tighter ecosystem work with partners such as Nvidia Corp. and Super Micro Computer Inc., and the organization’s hiring for a direct, results-driven culture. (* Disclosure below.).

Sources indicate that the way companies buy AI infrastructure has changed along with the technology. Deals at neocloud providers no longer go to a single enterprise buyer. They now involve the off-taker renting the capacity, the cloud operator and the integration software layer, Delane explained. Timelines have shrunk just as sharply, from six months to a year for a traditional enterprise sale to as little as 30 days.

“The sales cycle is more complex for sure. The speed is insane,” Delane noted. “Sometimes these things are 30 days and you have to be ready to turn things around and really work with your customers and partners rapidly.”.

DDN is answering with tighter ecosystem work. Its decade-long partnership with Nvidia anchors the strategy, and joint offerings with Super Micro, such as the Enterprise AI HyperPOD, aim to replace a data center buildout with a ready-to-run AI stack. At SC26, DDN also introduced software-defined EXAScaler deployment to give enterprise AI customers more choice of hardware.

“It takes the complexity out of it, allows an enterprise to set up an AI pod within 3 hours,” Delane said.

The performance case holds up in the public cloud too. On Google LLC’s Google Cloud, customers using DDN’s Managed Lustre service saw 70% better training performance and a 40% gain in overall GPU efficiency, Delane noted.

Industry observers note that DDN is growing threefold this year while adding only a few salespeople, leaning its hiring toward technical and implementation staff who can get customers up and running faster. Delane looks for grit and a fit with a direct, results-driven culture.

“If people can fit that culture, want to come in, want to grow this company to multiple billions, we have a place for them,” Delane said.

Recent findings suggest that could 2027 finally be the year Cardano (ADA) overtakes Ripple (XRP) in the cryptocurrency rankings? Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta AI predicts that, despite XRP’s established position among the industry’s largest digital assets, network upgrades, renewed institutional interest, and a shift in investor sentiment could make it more likely than it first appears.

In a recent development, both cryptocurrencies have spent years competing for attention, albeit with very different propositions. XRP has built its reputation around cross-border payments and financial infrastructure, while Cardano has focused on research-driven development, decentralized applications, and a carefully structured ecosystem.

However, market leadership can change quickly during a cryptocurrency bull market. If Cardano delivers on its ambitious development roadmap while XRP struggles to maintain its momentum, the gap between the two could narrow considerably.

And while flipping XRP would require an extraordinary rally, ADA could climb to a valuation few investors right now anticipate.

One of Cardano’s biggest opportunities heading into 2027 is its ongoing push to improve network scalability.

The planned Ouroboros Leios upgrade is particularly crucial. Designed to increase transaction throughput without compromising Cardano’s decentralized architecture, Leios could address a longstanding criticism: its ability to compete with higher-throughput blockchain ecosystems.

According to recent reports, cardano’s Dijkstra development cycle also introduces further improvements, with Peras activation targeted for the second quarter of 2027. Peras is designed to improve transaction settlement speed by reducing the time needed to achieve stronger confirmation confidence.

Meanwhile, developments around programmable tokens, decentralized finance, and real-world asset tokenization could help Cardano attract applications that generate genuine demand for ADA.

These upgrades won’t automatically translate into higher token prices, but successful implementation could give investors a compelling reason to reconsider Cardano’s long-term valuation.

XRP has several advantages that Cardano cannot easily replicate. Ripple has spent years building relationships across the financial sector, while the XRP Ledger continues to expand into institutional decentralized finance, stablecoins, and tokenized real-world assets.

The network processed an average of approximately 2.48 million daily transactions during the first quarter of 2026, while its real-world asset market capitalization reached $2.25Bn. These are meaningful indicators of ecosystem activity.

Industry observers note that however, XRP’s enormous market capitalization also creates a challenge for investors seeking outsized returns. With a much larger valuation than ADA, XRP needs substantially more capital inflows to achieve the same percentage gains.

Recent market comparisons have placed XRP’s valuation at roughly ten times Cardano’s, highlighting the scale of the challenge. If capital rotates toward smaller, established layer-1 networks during the next bull market, ADA could benefit disproportionately.

ADA previously reached an all-time high around $3.10 during the 2021 bull market, demonstrating that the cryptocurrency can attract substantial speculative demand when market conditions are favorable.

A sustained recovery towards its previous peak would be an notable psychological milestone. However, a genuine breakout beyond that region would potentially open the door to a much larger valuation.

For XRP, the challenge is maintaining its market leadership while competing with an expanding range of payment-focused blockchain networks. Its established institutional presence provides a strong foundation, but continued adoption growth will be necessary to justify a substantially higher valuation.

The key technical signal to watch for ADA is a sustained sequence of higher highs and higher lows on the weekly and monthly charts, accompanied by improving relative strength against XRP.

A decisive break above previous cycle resistance, followed by a successful retest, could signal that a longer-term trend reversal is underway.

Cardano successfully implements its major upgrades, DeFi activity expands, institutional interest improves, and investors begin viewing ADA as an undervalued alternative to larger blockchain assets.

However, overtaking XRP would depend on more than Cardano’s own performance. XRP’s valuation would also need to be considered, meaning ADA could reach $2.50 without necessarily overtaking its rival.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
WTW: Global health insurance costs set to rise 10.2% next year" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Global health insurance costs are set to rise by double digits in 2027 for the second straight year, according to a latest survey.

WTW released its latest Global Medical Trends Survey, which estimates that the average gross cost for medical benefits will increase by 10.2% in 2027. This follows a 10.1% increase in 2026 and a 9.8% increase in 2025, according to the report.

In the United States, the cost for medical benefits is expected to rise by 10.3% on average, on par with 2026 and up from a 9.4% increase in 2025. Across regions, the highest increases are expected in the Asia-Pacific, averaging 12.6% in 2027.

The next-highest region was North America, with a projected 10.5% average increase.

Sources indicate that the survey was conducted in June and August 2026 and includes responses from 393 insurers offering coverage across 92 countries. Just under half (49%) of those surveyed stated they anticipate elevated medical and pharmacy costs to impact them over the next three years, and likely persist beyond that window.

The WTW analysts mentioned this likely means that insurers will remain focused on cost containment and sharing measures in the near future.

"In the US, healthcare costs remain under sustained pressure from new medical technologies, specialty pharmaceuticals, and the rising use of GLP-1 therapies, alongside higher provider costs and the ongoing demands of chronic and complex conditions," stated Courtney Stubblefield, strategy and specialty leader in Health & Benefits at WTW in an announcement.

More than three quarters (76%) of the surveyed insurers named new medical technologies as the leading cost drive for both medical and pharmaceutical costs. Sixty-five percent cited provider fee increases, and 45% named pharmaceutical advancements.

Cancer was the leading condition driving costs, the survey found, with 62% naming it as the top cost condition. Sixty-one percent of those surveyed mentioned they have seen an increase in cancer diagnoses among individuals under age 40 when compared to the past two years.

However, when looking at the conditions where costs are growing the most swiftly, cardiovascular disease rises to No. 1, cited by 54% of the surveyed insurers. Cancer was second on this ranking, and named by 51%, while diabetes was third at 28%.

"To manage this, employers need a multiyear, multifaceted strategy that addresses pharmacy spending and high-cost conditions—such as cancer, cardiovascular disease and diabetes—while keeping care affordable and accessible for employees," Stubblefield said.

#167900. Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1193 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that an international research team has developed a new technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease.
  • Industry observers note that the technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain.
  • Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that an international research team has developed a new technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

Industry observers note that the technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the new approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants.

Recent findings suggest that parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

For some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

"The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers.".

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells.

The new technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

Sources indicate that "We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces.".

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

It has been revealed that "The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she says. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain.".

The process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice.

According to recent reports, to investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

According to recent reports, "Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an important target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease.".

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly notable because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

Industry observers note that after the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice demonstrated significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," claims Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Industry observers note that another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

According to recent reports, however, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

According to recent reports, one possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

The researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

"Nevertheless, we are convinced that the upcoming method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately.".

Sources indicate that beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a upcoming way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward latest approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

Inference pushes AI to smaller sites, making the data layer the deciding factor

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off.
  • It has been revealed that that shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation.
  • Industry observers note that “As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:09 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

Inference is moving to the center of enterprise AI spending, and the AI data layer is emerging as the piece that decides whether those investments pay off. As GPU costs climb and component shortages persist, the architecture behind AI is shifting from a handful of massive facilities toward a distributed web of smaller sites.

It has been revealed that that shift is putting storage companies with roots in high-performance computing at the center of the AI conversation. Turning data into insight at an acceptable cost now depends on a resilient, secure data engine built for GPU efficiency, according to Alex Bouzari (pictured), co-founder and chief executive officer of DataDirect Networks Inc.

Industry observers note that “As inference is off the charts in terms of utilization, the data layer is what makes a difference,” Bouzari mentioned. “Costs are skyrocketing. GPUs are becoming more and more powerful, but also more and more expensive.”.

Industry observers note that bouzari spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how inference, cost pressure and shortages are reshaping AI infrastructure. (* Disclosure below.).

The first wave of AI buildouts concentrated GPUs in large, power-hungry facilities. Inference changes that math because it needs to run close to users and their data, Bouzari explained. Communities are also pushing back on giant monolithic data centers, he added.

“Now, what is happening with inference, you need to supplement that with smaller footprints. Let’s call them data centers, 1 megawatt, 2 megawatt, 5 megawatts. And those need to reside where the action is taking place, where the autonomous driving is happening, where physical AI is happening, where the sensor data is,” Bouzari said.

Connecting small pods back to large AI factories requires a different approach to data. DDN is building a software layer that spans many types of hardware, a direction reflected in its recent move to free its EXAScaler file system from DDN’s own hardware. The goal is to squeeze more use out of very expensive gear, according to Bouzari.

“It is a software layer that needs to accommodate the different types of hardware because, look, the costs being so high, people want to be able to maximize the utilization over an extended period of time, just like it was in high-performance computing,” Bouzari said.

The scale of spending has changed dramatically. A couple hundred million dollars once funded the world’s fastest supercomputer but now buys 15 to 20 racks of equipment, Bouzari noted. Shortages of GPUs, memory and solid-state drives are colliding with tighter budget scrutiny.

It has been revealed that “On the one hand, you have budgetary constraints and the need to extract as much value as you can from your investment,” Bouzari mentioned. “On the other hand, you have the shortages. And so a data layer that can do a lot more with a lot less infrastructure, the smaller footprint is extremely valuable.”.

That thinking extends into the enterprise. DDN’s Enterprise AI HyperPOD packages CPUs, GPUs, networking and storage into a rack that can drop into existing corporate sites with available power. Keeping the pod on-premises also gives companies tighter control over their data, Bouzari explained.

“I think we’re entering an era where we will see a blossoming of smaller footprint pods being deployed in enterprises globally,” Bouzari remarked.

Bouzari framed the AI data layer as the counterpart to accelerated compute, with Nvidia Corp. supplying the processing and DDN supplying the data. As inference and agents take over, the data side carries more weight, he stated: “You need both to make it successful. But the data engine, I think, is becoming increasingly crucial as inference and agentic is really becoming the predominant way to utilize AI and get value out of it.”.

#167896. Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain

Ozempic and Mounjaro may have a surprising effect on your brain

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Popular medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, may have effects that extend beyond weight loss and blood sugar control.
  • To examine this possibility, researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen reviewed the existing scientific evidence at the invitation of the journal Science.
  • In a recent development, studies involving animals suggest that GLP-1 medications can influence learning and memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Popular medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, may have effects that extend beyond weight loss and blood sugar control. These drugs also influence biological processes involved in brain function, raising questions about whether they could help preserve memory and thinking abilities.

To examine this possibility, researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen reviewed the existing scientific evidence at the invitation of the journal Science.

In a recent development, studies involving animals suggest that GLP-1 medications can influence learning and memory. However, research involving humans has produced less consistent findings. Analyses of patient health records have found an association between GLP-1 treatment and a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes. These observational findings are encouraging, but they cannot determine whether the medications themselves are responsible for the lower risk.

More definitive results have also raised questions. In Novo Nordisk's EVOKE and EVOKE+ clinical trials, semaglutide failed to slow the progression of early Alzheimer's disease. Although the treatment affected several biological markers associated with Alzheimer's, those changes did not translate into a measurable slowing of the disease.

Why Weight Loss Drugs May Still Benefit the Brain.

Despite the disappointing Alzheimer's results, researchers believe GLP-1 medications could still offer cognitive benefits to certain groups of patients.

People living with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience difficulties with attention, planning, and the speed at which they process information. These cognitive problems are often associated with metabolic health and blood vessel function, suggesting they may respond differently to treatment than the changes caused by Alzheimer's disease.

Improving blood sugar regulation, metabolism, or vascular health could potentially help preserve cognitive abilities, even if the same medications cannot slow an established neurodegenerative disease.

Stina Börchers, the review's first author and a researcher affiliated with both the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen, emphasizes the need to determine whether starting treatment earlier could make a difference.

According to recent reports, "We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also crucial to identify which patients might benefit," states Stina Börchers.

Unlocking Fresh Treatments to Protect Memory.

Industry observers note that A central unanswered question is how GLP-1 medications might influence the brain. Their potential cognitive effects could result from improvements in metabolic health, direct actions within the brain, or a combination of both.

Understanding these mechanisms could help researchers identify which patients are most likely to benefit and potentially lead to medications designed specifically to support memory and other thinking abilities.

Christoffer Clemmensen, the review's senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity treatments to explore the connection between metabolism and the brain.

In a recent development, "Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering upcoming opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function," indicates Christoffer Clemmensen.

In a recent development, the researchers are calling for clinical trials that evaluate memory, attention, and other cognitive abilities beginning when patients first start treatment. Following these changes over time could help establish whether GLP-1 drugs genuinely protect brain function and clarify who might benefit most.

They also stress that treatment is not without potential drawbacks, particularly for older adults and people who are physically frail. Rapid weight loss can lead to a reduction in muscle mass, which may weaken physical function and offset some of the possible benefits.

Careful monitoring will therefore be essential as researchers investigate whether today's weight loss and diabetes medications could eventually provide new ways to protect the brain.
